title: FORTH: Grounding Tactile VLA Execution via Forward-Only Proxy-Control Pairing
comment: The code and models are open-sourced at https://github.com/Jordanlllll/FORTH
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are widely credited with force control, operating on the unverified assumption that proxy loss minimization implies physical force grounding. In this work, we demonstrate that this assumption breaks down at three core deployment levels: frozen visual backbones discard contact geometry, downstream losses mask token-level gradient alignment, and discrete indicators trigger optimization collapse. To address these disconnections, we present FORTH, a forward-only measurement harness and execution framework that explicitly pairs the optimization objective at each level with its physical control observable. FORTH incorporates three grounded pillars: a layer-local, forward-only tactile encoder that preserves spatial contact geometry without backpropagation, a token-parallel zeroth-order adapter enabling activation-space updates, and SlipGuard, a continuous tactile verification gate that fires on incipient slip. On an elasto-plastic structural shell, FORTH's closed-loop gate peaks at 29 times lower grip force than a monotone reflex ramp, preventing structural crush where the baseline leaves permanent deformation. Furthermore, FORTH matches state-of-the-art execution performance with a 97.6% average success rate across three evaluated LIBERO suites, while reducing peak activation memory by 7.12 times compared to a backpropagated step on the same backbone. Enhanced perception enables deeper physical intelligence.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are rapidly advancing from tabletop picking to contact-rich manipulation. To operate effectively under contact, state-of-the-art systems increasingly augment pretrained visual backbones with tactile or force sensing modalities li2026atvla,li2026forcevla2,feng2026tactilereflex,zhang2026retouch . Concurrently, tactile sensing hardware and representations have matured: optical tactile sensors, high-fidelity contact simulators, and learned representations provide policies with spatially resolved contact maps rather than scalar load readings lambeta2020digit,si2021taxim,wang2020tacto,george2024vital,xiang2026tactilesurvey . While an emerging family of tactile VLAs reports force-aware execution across tasks like insertion, wiping, and grasping cheng2025omnivtla,ayral2026reactive,chen2026ptld,mao2026vibeact,zhou2026touchworld,cheng2026learning,yuan2026dextacwam,zhang2026restacvla,min2026geometric,meng2026reach,krohn2026multires,zhang2026detac , performance across these systems is predominantly evaluated using a single proxy metric per task level. Such scalar metrics obscure the underlying physical reality: the critical quantities governing whether an object survives an episode are rarely measured or reported together. This discrepancy stems from a missing evaluation and reporting convention. Existing research programs address isolated compute and memory bottlenecks without closing this measurement gap. Layer-local learning objectives replace global backpropagation with forward-only computations hinton2022,li2024ffchip,ma2025ffint8,rub2025sparseff,jaiswal2026binaryff,nokland2019localerrorsignals,ren2022forwardgradient,krutsylo2025scalableff,gandhi2023extendingff,ororbia2023predictiveff,ahamed2023ffcontrastive , yet report performance strictly via local loss values. Zeroth-order (ZO) and gradient-free optimizers trade memory-intensive backward passes for forward queries ars,mezo,eggroll,vlazo,zoadamm,gautam2024vrzofinetune,zhang2025zoflatminima,shang2025zoquantized,yang2025sharpzo , evaluating only estimated gradient directional alignment. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and quantization constrain these updates within frozen backbones hu2021lora,dettmers2023qlora,houlsby2019adapters , while low-level controllers treat physical slip as a binary classification target scored by detection accuracy. Crucially, an improvement in these algorithmic proxies can decouple from physical interaction quality---a lower local loss does not inherently prevent object damage---and no current benchmark protocol liu2023libero,mees2021calvin,james2019rlbench,mandlekar2021robomimic,zhu2020robosuite,makoviychuk2021isaacgym,nvidia2025isaaclab,chi2023diffusionpolicy,octo2024,kim2025openvlaoft,xiang2026contactbench,higuera2024sparsh,tsai2023realitygap systematically measures and reports these paired dynamics. To resolve this decoupling, we introduce , a unified harness governed by a paired metric convention across all three execution levels: report the optimized algorithmic quantity alongside the physical quantity it aims to control, accepting a policy level only when both metrics move in lockstep. Operating entirely forward-only and layer-locally on frozen 4-bit backbones without global backward passes, integrates three key components: (1) a tactile feature trunk composed of two Forward-Forward (FF) blocks; (2) a token-parallel zeroth-order adapter of rank 8 attached to the action head; and (3) SlipGuard, a one-class shear-ratio gate with a bounded real-time corrector. Rather than introducing a massive new backbone, makes tactile policy execution measurable and correctable directly on edge deployment hardware, requiring only 16 forward passes per update ( tokens) instead of full backpropagation. This design yields a deployment-ready harness that acts dynamically before manipulation failure occurs. Empirically, the forward-only tactile trunk matches backpropagated representation accuracy; the zeroth-order updater fine-tunes the rank-8 adapter at a fraction of backward memory requirements; and SlipGuard converts incipient slip into a recoverable interaction across three slip severity regimes, where standard hand-tuned force ramps result in permanent object crush. Figure~ fig:frames illustrates our testbed for recording physical contact dynamics across three material bodies driven past their friction limits. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-Language-Action Policies sec:vla_policies sec:rel-vla Vision-language-action models predict an action sequence from an image and an instruction~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,brohan2023rt2 . Their scale comes from a pretrained multimodal backbone rather than from robot data, and the head that turns features into commands is small enough to adapt on one GPU. Alongside them sit action-chunking transformers for low-cost bimanual teleoperation~ zhao2023actaloha , tokenizers that compress a chunk to a short sequence~ pertsch2025fast and open-world variants of the recipe~ physicalintelligence2025,yang2026mantis,huang2026fastthinkact . Touch enters that stack in three ways: as semantic-aligned tokens projected into the same space as text~ cheng2025omnivtla , as a residual representation added to a frozen visual policy~ zhang2026restacvla , or as a predictive model that forecasts contact before it occurs~ zhou2026touchworld,yuan2026dextacwam,jing2026cand . Neighboring designs fuse heterogeneous tactile sensors behind one policy~ krohn2026multires,li2026atvla , learn the touch representation from future visual supervision~ cheng2026learning , or name material and object properties from touch without closing a control loop~ yu2025demonstrating . A separate line learns force implicitly rather than conditioning on it~ li2026forcevla2,gillman2026goalforce : grip strength emerges from the task reward~ openai2018dactyl,rubik2019,chen2026ptld , and the force in the logs is whatever the policy found sufficient. Forward-Only Update Rules sec:forward_only sec:rel-forward Forward-only learning replaces the backward pass with a local objective. Forward-Forward trains each layer on its own contrastive goodness~ hinton2022 , and the similarity kernel of layer representations contracts toward rank one with depth~ priceoflocality . Local error signals and forward gradients are the neighboring non-contrastive route~ nokland2019localerrorsignals,ren2022forwardgradient ; contrastive, predictive-coding and scalable variants extend it~ ahamed2023ffcontrastive,ororbia2023predictiveff,gandhi2023extendingff,krutsylo2025scalableff . On hardware, INT8, sparse, binary-stochastic and closed-box trainers report lower energy, memory or compute than backpropagation at the edge~ ma2025ffint8,rub2025sparseff,jaiswal2026binaryff,li2024ffchip,spyra2025 . Zeroth-order optimization estimates a descent direction from function evaluations alone, from the black-box attack estimator~ chen2017zoo and random search~ ars,eggroll through adaptive moments~ zoadamm to MeZO~ mezo , with variance-reduced variants~ gautam2024vrzofinetune and convergence analyses~ zhang2025zoflatminima . Applications reach VLA adaptation~ vlazo , quantized fine-tuning~ shang2025zoquantized and prompt tuning~ yang2025sharpzo . These methods are judged by downstream loss or recall. A population argument, in which independent per-token perturbations average out, predicts that estimator quality improves with token count; that prediction has not been measured against the true gradient on a physical signal. Adaptation and evaluation practice supply the rest: low-rank and quantized adapters~ hu2021lora,dettmers2023qlora,houlsby2019adapters , one-bit backbones~ wang2025bitvla , benchmarks and simulators~ liu2023libero,mees2021calvin,james2019rlbench,xiang2026contactbench,makoviychuk2021isaacgym,nvidia2025isaaclab,mu2025robotwin , and replication practice~ norton2024mirrer,vaughan2012publishcode,luo2026toward . Slip Detection and Tactile Sensing sec:tactile_sensing sec:rel-tactile Slip detection has a reflex-control literature that predates learned policies. Visuo-tactile classifiers run on multi-scale temporal convolutions~ gao2023visuo , and incipient-slip measurement tracks the transition during in-hand pivoting~ li2023incipient,romano2011grasp,boonstra2024incipient,sui2024incipient . Geometric reconstruction recovers extrinsic contact from touch and proprioception~ min2026geometric , and the same contact signal drives sub-millimeter insertion~ meng2026reach . A second class puts that signal in a fast loop under a slow planner: a reactive dexterous controller~ niu2026rex,ayral2026reactive , or a vibration signal routed straight to action~ mao2026vibeact . On the representation side the split is between an online-refined tactile prediction that absorbs contact drift~ zhang2026retouch and a decomposition that separates force from surface texture~ zhang2026detac . Both matter for the representation level: an aggregate can be predictive of contact and still carry no usable force. Evaluation in this line is detection rate, latency and false positives on a held-out session, which scores the detector while the force it commands can stay wrong. The substrate matured alongside the policies: gel-sensor hardware~ lambeta2020digit , simulators~ si2021taxim,wang2020tacto , visuo-tactile pretraining~ george2024vital , sim-to-real transfer~ tsai2023realitygap and a recent survey~ xiang2026tactilesurvey . title: MomentMem: Memorizing Key Moments for Robot Manipulation
summary: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering visual information that is no longer observable, such as the original location of an object. Existing approaches typically rely on full observation histories, which become redundant over long horizons, or text summaries, which may omit precise visual details. We study visual moment memory, the ability to retain such details from key moments for subsequent manipulation. To support this study, we introduce VMBench, a suite of long-horizon manipulation tasks requiring memory of spatial locations, visual appearances, and their associations. We further propose MomentMem, a hierarchical architecture in which a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes and an executor predicts actions conditioned on the selected memories. This separation enables us to evaluate memory selection alongside closed-loop task success and to study memorizer generalization independently of the executor. On VMBench, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points. Moreover, we find that the memorizer transfers well to unseen appearances zero-shot. It can also adapt to an unseen task with only a few memory annotations, reaching 43.7% success, close to the 44.3% obtained with full memory supervision. Further experiments show competitive performance on RMBench and improvements in real-robot manipulation. These results highlight the value of retaining sparse visual evidence for memory-dependent manipulation. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MomentMem.

Our code is available at . =-1 Introduction Recently, memory has increasingly become a key capability of multi-modal models~ moviechat,malmm,flashvstream,fluxmem and embodied models~ memoryvla,pam,memer,bpp . Despite advances in embodied models~ openvla,pi05,geminirobotics , memory for robot manipulation remains challenging. As shown in Figure~ fig:teaser (a), existing approaches often focus on full observation histories~ nativemem or text descriptions~ rmbench,pimem . Full observation histories are complete yet redundant, thus falling short when facing long-horizon tasks~ eventvla,fluxmem . Text captures abstract events, yet can omit visual details, or cannot fully describe certain information (e.g., ``move the cube back to where it was''). To this end, we study visual moment memory for robotic manipulation. It requires models to remember precise visual information at a key moment, such as texture patterns, spatial relations, and spatial locations. This type of memory is difficult to preserve in text. =-1 As a first step, we propose , a benchmark of long-horizon manipulation tasks that require visual moment memory. Its key design principle is to make successful manipulation depend on remembering precise visual information. Different from existing benchmarks~ mikasa,robomme,rmbench,robomemarena , our benchmark emphasizes tasks that cannot be well addressed by concise text memory. Specifically, these tasks require remembering exact positions and visual patterns, rather than only object identities or task progress. Concise text summaries may omit these details, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:teaser (b). We organize the tasks around spatial locations, visual appearances, and appearance-location bindings. For example, returning a cube to its original position requires remembering exactly where it was, rather than just knowing that it was moved. Across these tasks, the key visual moment is only visible across a short period of time and the model has to capture such moments for successful task completion. Together, these tasks provide a testbed for studying how robots memorize precise visual information for manipulation tasks. =-1 Going further, we consider the modeling of visual moment memory for robot manipulation. Task success alone does not reveal whether a failure comes from memory or execution~ memobench . Beyond overall task performance, we seek to examine two key capabilities: memory selection and action prediction. To this end, we propose , a hierarchical architecture that separates memory from action prediction. This separation allows us to examine memory selection and action execution independently. As shown in Figure~ fig:teaser (c) (top), a VLM memorizer selects keyframes, and then the executor predicts actions. We observe that the key event often spans across several frames that show the same visual cue. We annotate this span as a temporal segment. We aim for the memorizer to select a keyframe in the segment as early as possible. Also, if it misses an earlier frame, it should still try to capture the later frame in the same segment. During inference, the executor predicts actions from the selected keyframes together with the current observation. Details are provided in Section~ sec:methodology . =-1 With our benchmark tasks and hierarchical model, we design metrics and protocols to evaluate end-to-end success rate and the generalization of memory capability, as shown in Figure~ fig:teaser (c). As in most existing benchmarks, we test the models on our benchmark tasks and measure the success rate over closed-loop rollouts. We evaluate how well the memorizer captures the relevant evidence. We also test its transfer to unseen appearances and adaptation to new tasks. As shown in Figure~ fig:teaser (c) (bottom), we vary the visual appearance and directly test the overall model, with the memorizer trained only on the original visual appearances. Besides, we test the overall model for unseen tasks, allowing the memorizer to adapt to new tasks with a few memory annotations. In both protocols, we train the executor on target-domain action demonstrations using memories predicted by the memorizer. In other words, our protocols measure the generalization of the memorizer rather than the executor. =-1 On , achieves 49.9 average success, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points. RT-2~ rt2 transferred web-scale semantic knowledge to robotic control, while OpenVLA~ openvla and Octo~ octo developed open generalist policies trained on diverse robot data. Recent models, including ~ pi0 , ~ pi05 , GR00T series~ grootn1 , GigaBrain series~ gigabrain0,gigabrain05,gigabrain07 , and Gemini Robotics~ geminirobotics , improve action generation and cross-task generalization. =-1 Despite these advances, most VLAs condition on the current observation or a short context window. They therefore struggle when relevant evidence has disappeared from view~ pi0,memoryvla,kcvla,muvla . Our work addresses this limitation by providing VLA models with task-relevant keyframes identified from earlier observations. =-1 Robotic Manipulation Policies with Memory Some robotic manipulation tasks require evidence from earlier observations, motivating policies that use interaction history~ sam2act,memoryvla,rmbench . Available information includes the task instruction, visual observations, actions, and proprioceptive states. Existing memory methods differ in how they store and use historical information. Some methods maintain recurrent states, memory banks, or compressed tokens to retain information from long histories~ memoryvla,memoryvlapp,muvla,rememvla,rbvla,nativemem,echo,pam . Compressing long histories may discard visual details needed for later actions. Other methods summarize the history with language or use textual plans as memory~ rmbench,memer,pimem . Such representations are compact, but concise text summaries may omit task-relevant visual details, such as fine-grained appearances. Another line of work directly selects observations from the visual history~ bpp . This preserves raw visual evidence, though several methods select with predefined rules or heuristics~ kcvla,helm,kemo,robomemarena . Such rules may need adjustment when memory requirements change. =-1 Our method learns when to save observations that contain evidence needed for later actions. It uses a hierarchical architecture with separate memorizer and executor modules. The most closely related method is EventVLA~ eventvla , which predicts keyframes from predicted future actions within a single model. Our memorizer instead selects keyframes from visual observations independently of action prediction. =-1 Robotic Memory Benchmarks Several benchmarks evaluate memory in robotic manipulation. RMBench~ rmbench supports systematic evaluation of memory in robotic imitation learning. MIKASA-Robo~ mikasa and RoboMME~ robomme evaluate multiple dimensions of memory, while MemoryBench~ sam2act focuses on spatial memory and action recall. Other benchmarks focus on memory in long-horizon tasks, which involve extended trajectories and require precise manipulation~ robomemarena,eventvla,embodiedslotssm,prism . title: LoCo-WAM: Test-Time Training as Long Context for World-Action Models
summary: World-action models guide robot actions by predicting what happens next, but typically condition on a short observation history. Extending this history increases computation at every decision and can require a separately trained model. We introduce LoCo-WAM, which learns from the outcomes of its actions through test-time training while keeping the same short history length. It uses newly observed frames to update a low-rank adapter in the video expert, whose adapted predictions guide subsequent actions. The updates accumulate within each episode and are reset between episodes, allowing past observations to influence decisions after they leave the input window. LoCo-WAM thus learns from a longer stream of experience without expert action labels, additional data or meta-training. Experiments on two world-action models show improved task success across four simulation benchmarks. On RoboCasa GR-1, a model with 2.4,s of history matches one trained with 9.6,s, while a model with 4.8,s exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points. Our analysis shows that the updates improve prediction of upcoming frames, affect the action mainly through adaptation of the imagined future, and have an increasing effect on actions as the episode unfolds.

Introduction sec:intro Human behavior combines knowledge acquired over time with rapid learning from new experience, as described by complementary learning systems theory~ mcclelland1995complementary . In motor control, discrepancies between predicted and observed sensory outcomes can drive adaptation during action~ tseng2007sensory . These findings motivate learning during robot execution, where the outcomes of actions provide feedback for the predictions that guide subsequent behavior~ noh2025latent . World-action models~ unipi,uva,cosmospolicy,lingbotva,longwam provide a natural setting for such learning. They predict future frames together with actions, drawing on video pretraining to learn how scenes evolve. In the models we study, the imagined future guides action generation. After the robot acts, the observed frames provide targets for the model's own video loss. As interactions within a task share objects, surroundings and dynamics, learning from these frames may improve predictions of what happens next. The updated predictions can then guide subsequent actions. This learning allows experience to influence behavior beyond a fixed observation window. Most world-action models condition on a short history, which limits the past observations available at each decision. Extending the history~ longwam,lingbotva increases computation and can require a separately trained model. Selecting or compressing the history requires components that are trained together with the policy~ hilowam,memorywam,dimwam . Updating the model on the observed frames provides another way to use the past observations. These updates are a form of test-time training, a family of methods that update a model on each test input with a self-supervised loss~ ttt_sun , which has been extended to language and video generation models~ templora,slowfastvgen,ttte2e,tttlayers,oneminute . We introduce LoCo-WAM, a test-time training method for world-action models, which trains the video expert during execution with its video loss on the observed frames. At every decision, LoCo-WAM takes one gradient step on a low-rank adapter~ lora of the video expert to predict the most recently observed frames from the history that preceded them. It keeps the action expert unchanged and resets the adapter at the start of every episode. Since the adapter accumulates these updates over the episode, the video expert is trained on frames that have already left its history. The action expert then generates the next action from the imagined future and the features of the adapted video expert. LoCo-WAM thereby requires no labels, rewards, additional data, new layers or meta-training, keeps the history length of the model, and can run its update while the robot executes the current action chunk. We evaluate LoCo-WAM on two world-action models, Long-WAM~ longwam and LingBot-VA~ lingbotva , and four simulation benchmarks: RoboCasa GR-1~ gr00tn1 , RoboCasa365~ robocasa365 , LIBERO-Mem~ liberomem and RoboTwin 2.0~ robotwin2 . LoCo-WAM improves the base model on all four benchmarks. On RoboCasa GR-1, Long-WAM with 2.4\,s of history reaches 73.6 with LoCo-WAM, on par with the base model trained with 9.6\,s of history, at 0.76\,s per decision compared with 0.67\,s and without training a separate model. With 4.8\,s of history, it reaches 78.3 , 4.8 points above the 9.6\,s model ( ). On LIBERO-Mem, LingBot-VA with an 8-chunk history matches its default 30-chunk history. On both benchmarks, LoCo-WAM also outperforms test-time methods for robot policies, including AdaWorldPolicy~ adaworldpolicy , which adapts the world model across the episodes of a task, and RoboTTT~ robottt , which meta-trains fast-weight layers. Our analysis on RoboCasa GR-1 examines what an update of the video expert learns from the observed frames, how it reaches the action, and how its effect develops over the episode. The update improves the prediction of upcoming frames before they are used for training, with larger reductions in video loss for shorter histories. Using the model's own predictions as targets in place of the observed frames removes the gain in success rate. The update affects the action mainly through the imagined future, since applying it only when the video expert predicts this future recovers most of the gain. We further show that updating only the video expert performs better than also updating the action expert with the action loss. Over the episode, the change of the action accumulates, and stopping the updates early removes most of the gain. In summary, our contributions are: We introduce LoCo-WAM, test-time training as long context for world-action models: the video expert is trained during execution with its video loss on the observed frames, without labels, additional data or meta-training. On two world-action models and four simulation benchmarks, LoCo-WAM improves the base model on all four benchmarks, enables a model with a short history to match or exceed the base model with a longer history, and outperforms prior test-time methods for robot policies. We analyze how the update of the video expert reaches the action: it improves the prediction of upcoming frames from the observed frames, affects the action mainly through the imagined future, and the change of the action it causes accumulates over the episode. Related Work sec:related World-action models. World-action models predict future frames together with actions, which enables them to benefit from large-scale video pretraining and to use the predicted future to choose actions~ unipi,kong2026plan,kong2024latent,noh2025latent,cheng2025latent . Examples include UniPi~ unipi , GR-1~ gr1bytedance , VPP~ vpp , UVA~ uva , UWM~ uwm , Cosmos Policy~ cosmospolicy , OpenWAM~ openwam , Fast-WAM~ fastwam and LingBot-VA~ lingbotva , many of which pair a pretrained video model that predicts the future frames with an action model that generates the actions from this prediction. title: RoboDyna: A Benchmark for Evaluating Robotic Manipulation under Physically Grounded Dynamics
comment: 8 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Project page: https://robodyna.github.io/robodyna/
summary: Object manipulation in the dynamic real world requires understanding how the environment functions and evolves, and acting accordingly. Existing benchmarks, however, do not adequately address these needs. Physics-oriented benchmarks evaluate predictive fidelity but not closed-loop action. Dynamic robotic manipulation benchmarks often use simplified, physically implausible object motions, limiting evaluation of reasoning and action under realistic dynamics. Evaluation is also typically synchronized, freezing the environment during inference and making computation time irrelevant to task outcomes. To this end, we propose RoboDyna, a benchmark for evaluating the physical understanding and action capabilities of manipulation policies in dynamic scenes. RoboDyna comprises 20 conceptual dynamic tasks spanning five capability categories, with simple objects and minimal scene clutter, under a two-factor difficulty design, and 10 household tasks that instantiate the same capabilities in visually and semantically richer simulated real-world environments. RoboDyna provides 3,500 expert demonstrations, paired synchronous and asynchronous evaluation protocols, metrics for task success and partial completion, and interactive tools for human baseline evaluation. Evaluating vision-language-action models and a world-action model across 5.4K episodes, we find that all policies achieve success rates below 20%, revealing substantial limitations in dynamic manipulation. The world-action model captures simple physical dynamics but struggles with complex interactions, and its prediction fidelity does not consistently align with task success. Sync-async comparisons show that inference latency flips 5-12% of episode outcomes while changing average success rates by at most 3%. Introduction Recent robotic manipulation policies demonstrate impressive capabilities in static scenes~ black2024pi0,pi2025pi05,liu2023libero,nasiriany2024robocasa , but their physical competence in dynamic environments remains underexplored. Completing a task in a dynamic environment introduces two challenges~ fang2026domino,xie2026dynamicvla . First, selecting the correct action may require integrating multiple observations to infer object motion and anticipate future states. Second, the correct action must be executed within a critical time window, as scene evolution can render an otherwise valid action ineffective~ chen2026reflex,black2025rtc . Evaluating such physical competence requires both anticipating how the scene will evolve and acting accordingly. However, current benchmarks do not jointly evaluate both. Predictive world-model benchmarks~ nvidia2025cosmos,liao2025genie primarily evaluate physical consistency and the fidelity of predicted futures, with limited emphasis on closed-loop policy performance under realistic execution timing. Robotics benchmarks either contain no independent scene dynamics~ gu2023maniskill2,liu2023libero,nasiriany2024robocasa or animate targets with scripted motion while pausing the world during inference~ fang2026domino . Evaluating under the latter regime has several consequences. First, physically implausible dynamics limit transfer to real-world physics. Second, limited dynamic complexity restricts the range of physical capabilities tested. Third, synchronous evaluation makes inference cost-free: the environment is frozen during computation, whether a policy takes seconds per action chunk~ feng2025vidarc or runs at tens of hertz~ black2024pi0 . To this end, we propose , a physics-governed, latency-aware benchmark for dual-arm manipulation in dynamic environments (see Fig.~ fig:teaser ). challenges policies to anticipate scene evolution, accounts for inference latency, and jointly evaluates physical understanding and action capabilities. The proposed benchmark consists of 20 conceptual tasks, divided into five physical-understanding categories with varying difficulty levels to measure core policy competencies. An additional 10 complex household tasks are designed to evaluate transfer to realistic scenes. For evaluation, we use mixed metrics to record full and partial success under synchronous and asynchronous regimes. Moreover, our benchmark contains 3 , 500 expert demonstrations and tools for collecting human baseline performance under teleoperation and scene-interactive control. In summary our contributions are as follows: (1) we propose , a benchmark suite of physics-governed dynamic tasks, which consists of 20 conceptual tasks in five capability categories with four per-task difficulty designs and additional 10 household tasks; (2) We define a paired synchronous and asynchronous evaluation protocol to isolate the effect of inference latency on task outcome and mixed success and partial-success metrics; (3) We conduct extensive evaluation of two state-of-the-art VLAs and one WAM on over 5400 episodes to characterize their physical competence under different dynamic conditions; (4) We report on 12-participant human baseline performance on proposed tasks using different control regimes. Related Work sec:related Robotic Manipulation Policies Learning-based robotic action policies, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs)~ pi2025pi05,zheng2025xvla,black2024pi0,kim2024openvla and world-action-models (WAMs) liao2025genie,kim2026cosmospolicy,zheng2026motionwam,yuan2026fastwam , map images, language, and robot states to actions, with recent systems spanning flow-matching, autoregressive, and video-prediction-based designs. Standard evaluations primarily measure task success, often using a synchronous simulator or fixed action clock. While useful for comparing grounding and motor competence, such evaluations do not reveal whether a policy anticipates rolling, bouncing, or contact-induced motion, nor whether its computation finishes in time to act on such dynamics. We evaluate two VLAs, ~ pi2025pi05 and X-VLA~ zheng2025xvla , and one WAM, FastWAM~ yuan2026fastwam , to compare their performance on dynamic manipulation tasks. Predicting and Understanding Physics Video and world-model benchmarks evaluate future prediction using image or state fidelity, perceptual similarity, or physical-plausibility scores~ nvidia2025cosmos,liao2025genie,feng2025vidarc . These protocols assess whether a model can forecast how a scene will evolve, but not whether it can act successfully in that evolving scene. A visually accurate forecast can coexist with an action that is too late, misdirected, or dynamically infeasible, for example, causing unintended collisions between the robot and scene objects. Closed-loop efforts, such as World-in-World~ zhang2025worldinworld incorporate actions into prediction, yet do not evaluate robotic manipulation under continuous physical dynamics and measured inference latency. instead evaluates physical reasoning through action, testing whether policies can successfully manipulate objects under gravity, friction, contact, and continuous scene evolution. General-purpose suites, such as RoboDojo ~ chen2026robodojo , RoboCasa~ nasiriany2024robocasa , and LIBERO ~ liu2023libero evaluate complex manipulation, robustness, and long-horizon composition. Their canonical scenes are largely static, with scene changes driven primarily by the robot's actions rather than independent dynamics. Emerging benchmarks with object motion~ fang2026domino animate the targets of otherwise static tasks with scripted motion. The resulting dynamics are not physically plausible: objects translate sideways or drift randomly through the scene, unconstrained by gravity or friction. instead builds its tasks around physically grounded dynamics. Five capability categories cover complex motion in which objects roll, bounce, slide, and spin under gravity and friction (Section~ sec:benchmark ). Across these settings, we probe how policy performance degrades with increasing dynamic complexity. Standard robotic manipulation benchmarks typically freeze the world during policy inference. Under this synchronous convention, a slow policy receives the same state as a fast one, removing the need to account for scene evolution during inference. Concurrent asynchronous protocols~ xie2026dynamicvla,chen2026reflex relax this assumption, but do not provide a paired synchronous/asynchronous evaluation on identical physics-grounded episodes. fills this gap by replaying identical seeds under synchronous and asynchronous protocols, where the latter allows the scene to evolve during policy inference. This paired evaluation isolates the effect of inference latency on task performance. Trajectory prediction requires anticipating the future position of objects undergoing continuous motion, including motion redirected by contact or collision. title: FoRe: A Force-Guided Framework for Autonomous Grasp Recovery in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance in grasp-based manipulation, yet reliable recovery from local grasping failures remains challenging. Specifically, in pick-and-place tasks, policies may continue transport after a failed grasp instead of retrying, potentially reflecting overreliance on proprioceptive cues for stage progression and limited retry supervision. Existing recovery approaches typically rely on deployment-time guidance or demonstration augmentation. We introduce Force-guided Recovery (FoRe), a framework for autonomous recovery from local grasping failures. Using force feedback, FoRe partitions demonstrations into approach-grasp and transport-placement stages to train separate policies. To supplement limited retry supervision, FoRe then initializes a dedicated retry policy from the approach-grasp policy and refines it through local reinforcement learning (RL) from post-failure states. To avoid inappropriate stage progression, a controller combines force feedback with grasp-command status at inference to coordinate the stage policies, detect grasp failures, and invoke the retry policy. We also construct LIBERO-SUCTION, a force-augmented suction manipulation benchmark adapted from LIBERO, with complete demonstration trajectories for policy training. FoRe consistently improves task success rates for VLA-Adapter and $π_{0.5}$ on LIBERO-SUCTION, LIBERO, and real-world tasks. On LIBERO-SUCTION, average absolute gains are 18.4% and 6.5%, respectively. The corresponding real-world absolute gains are 25.0% and 21.7%. FoRe also remains effective with only one demonstration per task on both simulation benchmarks.

Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage pretrained visual-language knowledge and diverse robot data for generalizable manipulation~ RT2,OpenVLA,OXE,BridgeV2,DROID , with advances in action generation, spatial understanding, reasoning, and long-horizon manipulation~ pi0,pi05,OpenVLA-OFT,SpatialVLA,CoTVLA . However, especially in pick-and-place tasks, reliable recovery from local execution errors remains challenging: an imitation-trained VLA policy may continue transport after a failed grasp, instead of retrying~ RLGeneralization,FLARE . Such behavior can turn a recoverable local error into overall task failure, motivating autonomous retries and task resumption. Two related limitations may explain why VLA policies fail to recover after an unsuccessful grasp. First, as shown in Fig.~ fig:question , manipulation tasks can be viewed as sequences of stages, such as the approach–grasp stage and the transport–placement stage, each with its own distinct objective. Because robot proprioceptive states often correlate with task progress in successful demonstrations, a policy may rely excessively on these proprioceptive state cues to transition to the corresponding stage, regardless of the actual grasp outcome~ CausalConfusion,FLARE . Consequently, after a failed grasp, a robot proprioceptive state resembling those associated with transport may prompt the policy to persist in generating transport actions rather than retrying the grasp. Second, training dominated by uninterrupted successful demonstrations provides limited supervision for interrupting nominal execution and re-approaching the object after failure~ FLARE . The policy may therefore lack an effective response even when failure cues are observable. Recent studies have explored several approaches for robotic recovery. One direction uses human feedback~ RTH,YellRobot,OLAF or vision-language model (VLM) guidance~ AHA,FailSafe,ViFailback,CycleVLA to monitor execution outcomes and guide stage progression. Another direction augments demonstrations~ FLARE with varied robot poses and corrective trajectories to weaken correlations between pose and task progress and expand retry supervision. Force feedback provides direct physical cues about contact and load changes, making it an effective signal for detecting grasp failures. However, an explicit mechanism that uses such feedback to coordinate grasp retries and task resumption in VLA policies remains underexplored. We introduce Force-guided Recovery (FoRe), a framework for autonomous recovery from local grasping failures in VLA-based manipulation. FoRe first uses force feedback to partition successful demonstrations into approach–grasp and transport–placement stages, training a separate policy for each. To supplement limited retry supervision, FoRe then initializes a dedicated retry policy from the approach–grasp policy and refines it through local reinforcement learning (RL) from post-failure states. To avoid inappropriate stage progression, a controller combines force feedback with grasp-command status at inference to coordinate the stage policies, detect grasp failures, and invoke the retry policy. FoRe thus mitigates the adverse effects of relying on proprioceptive cues for stage progression through explicit stage control, while local retry learning supplements limited recovery supervision. Our main contributions are threefold: We propose FoRe, a framework that integrates independent training of two stage-specific policies, local refinement of a dedicated retry policy, and force-guided stage control to enable autonomous grasp recovery across VLA backbones. To support research on autonomous grasp recovery in suction-based manipulation, we construct LIBERO-SUCTION, a force-augmented benchmark adapted from LIBERO, comprising 22 tasks across three suites and 1,100 complete demonstrations for VLA training. The benchmark and demonstrations will be publicly released. We demonstrate that FoRe yields consistent improvements in task success with VLA-Adapter and , on LIBERO-SUCTION, LIBERO, and real-world tasks. Further evaluations show that FoRe also remains effective with only one demonstration per task on both simulation benchmarks. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-language-action (VLA) models have substantially advanced robotic manipulation by transferring pretrained visual and linguistic knowledge to action generation~ RT2 . OpenVLA~ OpenVLA demonstrates strong language grounding and adaptation to new tasks, while OpenVLA-OFT~ OpenVLA-OFT further improves task performance and inference efficiency. ~ pi0 and ~ pi05 extend VLA capabilities to dexterous control and long-horizon manipulation in diverse environments. SpatialVLA~ SpatialVLA incorporates 3D spatial representations to improve spatial understanding, while CoT-VLA~ CoTVLA introduces visual chain-of-thought reasoning by predicting intermediate goal images before action generation. Despite their strong generalization within the training task distribution, these models have limited autonomous recovery capabilities. Consequently, minor execution errors can escalate into task failures, substantially compromising the reliability of VLA task execution. Failure Recovery in Robotic Manipulation Human-guided approaches use language feedback to redirect execution and improve robot policies. RT-H~ RTH supports interventions through language descriptions of low-level motions, while Yell at Your Robot~ YellRobot incorporates real-time verbal corrections into hierarchical policies. OLAF~ OLAF uses verbal corrections to relabel actions for policy updates. Obtaining such corrective feedback requires human participation, which can limit scalability. VLM-based approaches automate failure analysis and recovery guidance: FailSafe~ FailSafe predicts recovery actions, and CycleVLA~ CycleVLA combines VLM-guided subtask backtracking with minimum Bayes risk decoding for retries. FLARE~ FLARE combines learned retries with reset skills invoked by an online multimodal monitor, while ReCoVLA~ ReCoVLA uses VLM-based failure detection to activate residual recovery policies. Online VLM supervision can introduce additional inference overhead and latency~ CycleVLA . In contrast to these approaches, FoRe introduces a novel and physically grounded approach to autonomous grasp recovery, using force feedback and grasp-command status to govern stage transitions, detect grasp failures and activate a retry policy refined through local RL. ConRFT and RECAP study RL-based post-training for real-world policy improvement~ ConRFT,RECAP . PLD trains residual specialists to collect recovery trajectories for fine-tuning the base policy~ PLD . SRPO uses model-generated successful trajectories as references for progress-based rewards on failed attempts~ SRPO . Compared to the above works, FoRe incorporates RL as a local refinement step within a broader recovery framework, optimizing only a dedicated retry policy from post-failure states. title: RoboColiseum: Co-evolution of Simulation, Evaluation, and Models
comment: 11 pages, 8 figures. The first eight authors contributed equally. Maoqing Yao and Qian Wang are the corresponding authors
summary: Simulation-based evaluation of embodied models requires calibrated interactions, diverse tasks, and explicit execution constraints. We present RoboColiseum, a platform combining system identification, composable physics and rendering, and multidimensional benchmarking. Recorded-command replay characterizes robot dynamics and object interactions, while a shared interface connects rigid and deformable simulation to rendering. Across 22 paired real--simulation robot--task configurations, task scores have a reported Pearson correlation of 0.9686. Eight evaluation tracks span instruction following, spatial reasoning, general manipulation, robustness, dexterous manipulation, precision manipulation, whole-body coordination, and execution across robot embodiments. Budget-aware scoring combines task progress, resource use, and completion rewards. We report 12 selected Season~I policies and all 11 systems on the public Season~II leaderboard, comprising eight Agent systems and three VLA policies. Agent2Act connects language models to robot-control execution; the VLA study uses mixed-task supervised fine-tuning. The results reveal substantial variation across tracks within each evaluation category. RoboColiseum connects simulation development with capability-oriented evaluation and provides a foundation for extending robot interactions and model assessment.
full_text: Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi0 and world action models (WAMs)~ ye2026dreamzero motivate evaluation that connects instruction understanding with physical execution. Simulation provides repeatable task instances and access to interaction diagnostics, but its usefulness depends on the relation between simulated and real behavior, the interactions it represents, and the information and computational resources available to the evaluated system. Three challenges motivate our design. First, physical plausibility of identified parameters does not by itself establish accurate task behavior. Physically consistent inertial identification~ wensing2018physicalconsistency and object parameter estimation~ he2026rigpi provide tools for calibration, while paired real--simulation evaluation is needed to assess the resulting task scores. Second, rigid and deformable interactions require different numerical representations and contact models. SoftMAC~ liu2024softmac and Embedded IPC~ du2024embeddedipc illustrate approaches to coupled interaction and computational efficiency. A common interface can make different backends accessible without assuming identical physical behavior or support for every backend combination. Third, evaluation must distinguish reasoning, execution, and resource use. VLABench~ zhang2025vlabench , EmbodiedBench~ yang2025embodiedbench , and EmbodiedEval~ cheng2025embodiedeval motivate broader interactive evaluation. Agent2Act~ robocoliseum2026agent2act evaluates multimodal models by having them directly generate robot-control commands through shared observation, execution, and feedback interfaces. The evaluated agent includes both the model and its execution harness. RoboColiseum focuses on three components. System identification and recorded-command replay characterize robot response and object interaction under stated control and observation settings. A shared protocol separates physics from rendering and supports backend-specific rigid and deformable representations. An eight-track benchmark retains instruction following, spatial reasoning, general manipulation, and robustness as Season~I, and adds dexterous manipulation, whole-body coordination, precision manipulation, and cross-embodiment transfer as Season~II. We assess RoboColiseum through paired Real2Sim experiments and public benchmark results. Season~I retains four foundational tracks~ yin2026seasoni ; Season~II introduces four additional capability dimensions. We report separate results for eight Agent systems and three VLA policies, preserving their respective training and execution settings. Agent2Act~ robocoliseum2026agent2act connects language-model reasoning to robot-control execution. The evaluation protocol specifies hidden layouts, execution budgets, and submission review. These components support a development cycle in which task-level observations motivate changes to simulation, training data, and evaluation coverage. We separate the robot dynamics, object interaction parameters, and execution settings so that each can be evaluated under a stated configuration. Introduction sec:intro Humanoid robots offer the potential to extend manipulation beyond fixed workspaces, enabling tasks that require coordinating object interaction with whole-body locomotion. For example, carrying a box through a narrow gap requires maintaining a stable grasp while aligning the torso and limbs with the opening and avoiding surrounding obstacles. Such behaviors depend on understanding the spatial relationship between the robot's body and the environment, as well as anticipating how this relationship will evolve during motion. Recent humanoid vision-language-action (VLA) models make these behaviors increasingly learnable from demonstrations and language instructions, typically by combining a vision-language backbone (System-2), a fast action generator (System-1), and a learned whole-body controller (System-0)~ bjorck2025gr00t,jiang2025wholebodyvla,wei2026psi0 . Despite this progress, humanoid VLA policies typically rely on head-mounted egocentric cameras, which provide limited cues for whole-body spatial awareness and future-oriented decision-making. The limitation is both spatial and temporal. Spatially, the egocentric view moves with the robot and can be occluded by its arms or carried objects, making it difficult to infer critical body--scene relationships, such as the distance between the shoulders and nearby obstacles, the alignment of the body with a narrow opening, or the robot's position relative to a junction. Temporally, policies are typically conditioned on current observations without explicit supervision for how these spatial relationships evolve as the robot moves. However, successful loco-manipulation requires anticipating the consequences of ongoing motion, rather than relying solely on what is visible in the current frame. These observations motivate extending the policy's perception beyond the egocentric view in both space and time. No existing benchmark fits this setting: ego-exo datasets are human and offline, while robot multi-view benchmarks target tabletop manipulation. We propose , which combines exocentric spatial context with dual-view foresight. For the spatial extension, we introduce a synchronized view from an additional exocentric camera. We encode this view with frozen DINOv3~ simeoni2025dinov3 and concatenate the resulting tokens with egocentric VLM tokens as input to the action expert ( ). This provides additional visual context about the scene layout and the robot's body relative to its surroundings. For the temporal extension, we use future observations from both views as privileged training supervision~ vapnik2009lupi . A residual adapter refines VLM latent features before they are passed to the action expert. A foresight expert reads the adapted features together with exocentric features and predicts frozen DINOv3 representations of both views 0.6\,s ahead ( ). The foresight loss supervises the observation interface, while the action expert is trained with flow matching. At deployment, we discard the foresight expert and retain the 4.2M-parameter adapter. We therefore build HELM, a benchmark of five simulated humanoid loco-manipulation tasks, with 50 paired in-distribution trials and 200 held-out scenes spanning layout, asset, material, lighting, and combined shifts. We evaluate our designs in closed-loop simulation over this benchmark. achieves full avg in-distribution and full avg under distribution shift, improving over both the egocentric baseline ( psi avg and psi avg ) and the no-foresight baseline ( s1 avg and s1 avg ). Target-space ablations show that predicting DINOv3 features of both views provides the strongest transfer, whereas predicting VLM features does not improve over the no-foresight baseline. title: SonoAtlasWorld: Anatomy-Grounded Ultrasound World Models for Wide-Range Scanning
comment: Interactive video demonstrations are available at: https://sonoatlasworld.github.io/SonoAtlasWorld
summary: Learning robotic ultrasound policies requires interactive environments for scalable data generation and repeatable evaluation, while exploration on real patients is limited by acquisition costs and safety constraints. Generative world models offer an alternative, but image history and probe actions alone do not ensure anatomical consistency across wide-range scans and changing acoustic windows. We introduce SonoAtlasWorld, an ultrasound world model built on anatomy as state. A persistent 3D anatomical asset extracted from computed tomography (CT) anchors each scan to a specific anatomy. Probe actions determine anatomical and acoustic visibility conditions for a causal ultrasound generator trained on clinical videos. Our three-stage pipeline combines anatomy-conditioned pretraining, causal conversion and long-rollout alignment. Inference optimizations achieve pose-to-ultrasound throughput of 81.2 FPS. To evaluate anatomical control beyond image similarity, we introduce the Action-Following Index (AFI), which measures normalized reconstruction gain over a static-prefix baseline. On 40 held-out 3D volumes, SonoAtlasWorld achieves liver and macro-organ AFI of 0.428 and 0.262, compared with at most 0.117 and 0.038 for the tested action- and geometry-conditioned methods. Long-rollout alignment reduces brightness drift by 3.46x at the end of 40 repeated scan cycles. SonoAtlasWorld also generates offline policy-training demonstrations and supports anatomically grounded closed-loop evaluation. Scaling the generated training data improves key-plane acquisition success from 48.2% to 81.2% on unseen anatomies in simulation, demonstrating its utility for robotic ultrasound policy learning.

Introduction sec:intro Ultrasound provides real-time imaging for diagnosis and intervention, yet acquiring diagnostic views depends strongly on operator expertise. Robotic ultrasound offers a route to more reproducible examinations, reduced physical workload and improved access where experienced sonographers are scarce~ jiang2023roboticultrasound . Autonomous scanning requires policies that coordinate image interpretation and probe motion across patient anatomies. Their development depends on realistic interactive environments for generating demonstrations and evaluating alternative actions. Constructing these environments remains difficult. Patient scans provide clinical observations, but repeated trial-and-error exploration is constrained by safety and practical considerations. Phantoms offer controlled interaction with limited anatomical diversity; physics-based simulators must balance image fidelity and computational cost~ burger2013gpu,salehi2015simulation,ao2025sonogym . Re-slicing reconstructed ultrasound volumes remains bounded by the acquired anatomy and viewing angles~ lasso2014plus . Learning from recorded scans also faces a data bottleneck: routine videos lack probe poses, and synchronized tracking requires calibration and dedicated acquisition protocols~ yang2026sonoworld,yang2026ultraworld . Generative world models offer a data-driven approach to interactive simulation, as illustrated by DreamDojo and Cosmos~ gao2026dreamdojo,nvidia2025cosmos . In ultrasound, SonoWorld grounds probe actions through EM-tracked clinical scans~ yang2026sonoworld , whereas UltraWorld uses synthetic supervision and geometric conditioning without real pose annotations~ yang2026ultraworld . A central challenge is preserving a specific anatomy throughout interaction, including when observation history provides an incomplete or ambiguous spatial reference. In wide-range liver scanning, a large organ and branching vasculature are viewed through changing cross-sections and acoustic windows. A vessel may leave the imaging plane or disappear behind rib or gas shadowing, then reappear from another acoustic window. Recent history may therefore contain only partial or acoustically obscured views, while distant anatomical regions can have similar appearances. Models relying solely on image history and probe actions must infer both unobserved anatomy and its correspondence across these views. Such cases challenge the preservation of anatomical identity through learned action--appearance correlations alone, motivating a persistent 3D anatomical reference during interaction. We introduce SonoAtlasWorld, an anatomy-grounded ultrasound world model built on the principle of anatomy as state. A 3D anatomical asset persists throughout the scan, and probe actions determine the cross-section and acoustic visibility sampled from it. A learned causal observation model generates ultrasound from these conditions and its observation history. Clinical videos provide appearance and temporal priors, while the retained anatomical asset provides the spatial reference for new scan trajectories. Anatomy and visibility conditioning support exploration across vessels, ribs and gas shadows ( ). To realize this anatomy-grounded formulation as an interactive environment, we develop a three-stage learning framework that combines an anatomy-conditioned ultrasound prior, a causal observation generator and long-rollout alignment ( ). The resulting model supports anatomically consistent, interactive ultrasound generation with reduced long-rollout drift. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce anatomy as persistent world state, separating persistent patient-specific spatial state from framewise observation conditioning. Probe actions dynamically sample spatially consistent anatomy and acoustic visibility from this shared 3D state across scan trajectories. We develop a three-stage training pipeline for causal generation and long-rollout alignment, and accelerate pose-to-ultrasound generation to 81.2 FPS for real-time wide range interactive scanning. We introduce an anatomy-referenced evaluation protocol for ultrasound world models, assessing anatomical action following, cross-trajectory consistency, and long-horizon stability. We further introduce the Action-Following Index (AFI) to measure anatomical agreement beyond a static-prefix baseline, complementing conventional image-quality metrics. summary: Visual labeling of egocentric demonstrations often leaves contiguous gaps in action supervision. Reliable poses around a gap still provide its net translation and rotation. We use this information to train vision-language-action policies while preserving ordinary flow matching on reliable local actions. A composition objective constrains the aggregate motion of missing-action estimates, combining multiple fixed windows when a gap exceeds the policy horizon. A shared interval branch learns from reliable endpoints and supplies the composition target. On LIBERO with 20% of demonstrations and 70.5% missing actions, the main method achieves 87.9% mean success over three training runs. In one paired comparison with matched observation exposure and training cost, its advantage over masking is 10.5%. On Ego-informed RoboTwin gaps, success is 45.4%, versus 40.3% for masking. On five real-robot tasks, mean success is 59.6%, versus 54.8% for interval flow matching alone and 48.8% for masking.

title: Portable Active Recovery under Timed and Position-Dependent Visual Outages
summary: When a camera blackout depends on physical position rather than elapsed time, stable hovering prevents visual recovery and mission completion. On stereo visual-inertial quadrotors without external localization, an exogenous timed blackout and an endogenous position-dependent dark zone appear identical at loss onset yet require opposite responses: hover-and-wait completes 93/96 timed blackouts but 0/96 spatial outages (13 hard failures), whereas blind continuation traverses many spatial zones yet fails heavily during timed blackouts. We formulate visual-outage recovery as a worst-condition active-observability problem and introduce a portable recovery module at the reference interface of an unchanged host controller with zero retraining. Using deployable telemetry alone, the module coordinates visual-loss detection, jerk-limited braking, bounded backward probing, settled rejoining, height-integral trim, and an optional gated prior-map branch. On a preregistered 48-scene benchmark (1,920 flights), our full MPPI configuration reaches 88.5% [81.2, 94.8] worst-condition completion, outperforming development-selected DATT-L1 by +29.2 pp [17.7, 40.6] and exceeding all six external baselines after Bonferroni correction. Attached without retraining to SimpleFlight, the module lifts worst-condition completion by +17.7 pp [7.3, 28.1] to 86.5% (and 90% across 1.0x/1.25x speeds, 0/80 hard failures). Trace diagnostics reveal that survival hinges on visual-inertial re-acquisition asymmetry at vision return -- not blind IMU drift suppression - and uncover a bias-drift map crossover confirmed on 72 held-out EuRoC windows.

Introduction sec:intro When a stereo visual-inertial quadrotor loses usable camera frames, stable hovering is not task recovery. Modern learned and adaptive flight controllers track agile trajectories with high accuracy while pose estimates remain available~ kaufmann2023champion,song2023racing,oconnell2022neuralfly,huang2023datt,chen2025simpleflight , yet multi-second visual blackouts force open-loop inertial propagation while the tracker keeps acting on drifting states. Under deployable onboard telemetry, two outage regimes are observationally aliased at loss onset yet impose opposite recovery laws. In an exogenous timed blackout ( , 8\,s), camera frames return automatically once the interval expires; stopping on inertial propagation preserves local visual context and completes 93/96 flights ( ). In an endogenous position-dependent dark zone ( , 1.35\,m arc), frames return only after the vehicle physically leaves the unobservable region; hovering inside the zone completes 0/96 flights (13 hard failures). Conversely, continuing blindly along the schedule traverses many spatial zones yet incurs 7--12 timed-outage hard failures across external trackers. Completing missions reliably when the outage mechanism is undisclosed requires an active-observability decision layer~ bajcsy1988active,kaelbling1998pomdp above low-level tracking, analogous to Simplex runtime assurance~ sha2001simplex . We decouple active recovery from low-level actuation at the reference interface, enabling zero-retraining deployment above unchanged host controllers. Beyond closed-loop recovery performance, trace-level diagnostics overturn a widely held intuition: stopping succeeds not by slowing open-loop IMU drift---which grows at a similar quadratic rate across actions and hosts ( \,cm difference at 4\,s despite higher body-rate excitation on MPPI)---but by governing visual-inertial re-acquisition when stereo frames return. Stopping or probing back into previously observed texture enables Basalt's KLT optical flow to collapse accumulated blind error to 2--8 , whereas forward traversal onto unseen far-side texture induces host-dependent re-acquisition jumps that a gated prior-map branch corrects on MPPI. Contributions. This paper makes three contributions: Worst-condition aliased-outage formulation and kinematic analysis ( ): We formalize timed versus position-dependent visual-outage recovery under parallel physical ( ) and localization-qualified ( , ) task-completion criteria scored by worst-condition completion , accompanied by a 1D kinematic lemma establishing exact quintic stopping depth, probe-budget feasibility, and two-segment blind-exposure reduction. Portable reference-interface recovery module ( ): Operating solely on deployable telemetry and references without altering host weights, our module coordinates visual-loss detection, jerk-limited braking, bounded backward probing (0.50\,m planned budget), settled rejoining, height-integral trim, and an optional support- and consistency-gated ORB-SLAM3 translation branch across three distinct flight controllers. Preregistered benchmark, cross-host transfer, and mechanistic diagnostics ( ): Across 48 fresh scenes (1 , 920 flights), the full MPPI configuration reaches 88.5 [81.2, 94.8] worst-condition , beating development-selected DATT-L1 by [17.7, 40.6] (H1) and all six external baselines under Bonferroni correction (99.17 ). Without retraining, the module lifts completion across MPPI, SimpleFlight, and DATT-L1, raises SimpleFlight worst-condition completion by [7.3, 28.1] to 86.5 (and 90 across speeds with 0/80 hard failures), and uncovers the re-acquisition asymmetry and bias--drift map crossover confirmed on real EuRoC data. title: Tripwire: Robot Agents that Program Their Own Interrupts under Human Disturbance
summary: Agent harnesses are turn-based: the agent acts, waits for the result, then reasons. When the action invokes a pretrained robot policy, such as a vision-language-action (VLA) or world action model (WAM), the policy may react continuously to observations, but the agent cannot revisit its decision until the call returns. Meanwhile, a person may step into the robot's path or move the object it is about to grasp. Invoking the agent more often narrows this blind interval, but a reasoning model takes seconds per decision and most control steps need no new one. We propose TRIP, a training-free, event-driven harness in which the agent programs its own interrupts. With each call, the agent writes a tripwire: a lightweight, stateful Python program that runs alongside the policy, can query a compact VLM (for example, to locate a person and measure their distance), and decides whether the call continues or control returns to the agent. When it fires, the harness halts the policy and returns control with the reason; the agent then reassesses, adapts, and continues under a rewritten tripwire. We evaluate TRIP with three VLAs and one WAM on RoboHD, a benchmark of 168 RoboCasa365 scenes in which a simulated person disturbs the robot and any human-robot contact counts as failure. Compared with a turn-based harness using the same agent and tools, TRIP halves the rate of human contact with the strongest policy, raising safety from 61.3% to 81.3%, without sacrificing task success (38.7% vs. 31.0%). Real-robot experiments show that TRIP completes two manipulation tasks under human interference where the turn-based harness and the policy alone largely fail.

Introduction sec:intro Frontier vision-language models increasingly act as agents for robots: they interpret scenes, decompose tasks, and coordinate execution through tool calls~ team2026systematically, yang2026astranomy, chen2026showharness, wang2026auriga . A common harness exposes a pretrained manipulation policy as a callable skill and invokes the agent again only when the call returns~ zhang2026harnessvla . This turn-based interface locks the agent out while the policy runs, even though an action chosen at the start of a call can become unsafe or obsolete before it finishes. If a person steps into the robot's path mid-execution, the agent remains blind to the disturbance until control is handed back. The policy's own closed loop does not remove this blind spot. Vision-language-action (VLA) models~ black2024pi_0, intelligence2025pi_, bjorck2025gr00t and world action models (WAMs)~ ye2026world can react to new observations, but strong performance when nothing interferes with the task does not guarantee reliable behavior around people. In a shared kitchen, someone may move the target plate or close the fridge door the robot has just opened. When we augment RoboCasa365 tasks~ nasiriany2026robocasa365 with a reactive human avatar, all four pretrained policies we evaluate lose more than half of their successes; the strongest drops from 61.9 to 20.8 and touches the person in roughly half of all episodes. The agent can interpret such disturbances and choose a response, but it needs timely access to the changing scene. Querying it more frequently incurs substantial computation, and each high-level decision still requires an inference call that can take seconds~ team2026systematically, yang2026astranomy . Watching the scene does not require strong reasoning: noticing that a person has come close is a perception problem that a compact VLM and a depth image settle in a fraction of a second. Existing systems watch a running call in one of three ways. VoLo~ chen2026volo polls a frontier model every few seconds. DoReMi~ guo2024doremi asks a small VLM whether language constraints written by the planner still hold: it can look for anything the planner names, but it gets back only yes or no. Code-as-Monitor~ zhou2025code runs generated code over geometric states tracked from the start of a subgoal, without issuing new VLM queries during execution. Reacting to a person takes both: spotting someone who was not in the scene when the check was written, and judging from their distance and motion whether they matter. What should interrupt the agent also shifts with its latest decision. After judging that a nearby person does not obstruct the task, the agent resumes the policy and needs to hear only if the person comes closer; if it chooses to wait, it instead needs to know when the person leaves. We let the agent program the interrupt and update it as its decisions change. We introduce TRIP ( ), a harness in which robot agents program their own interrupts. The agent attaches a tripwire to a tool call: a stateful Python program that runs alongside policy execution, direct robot motions, or waiting. A tripwire both looks and computes: it chooses which cameras to read and what to ask a compact VLM, such as where a person is, and combines the answer with depth, memory of earlier checks, and timers to decide whether to interrupt. When it fires, the harness halts the active call before waking the agent with the reason, so stopping costs one check (0.24\,s on average on our real robot) and not an agent turn (4.3\,s). The agent then resumes the policy, repositions the robot, or waits, updating the tripwire as needed so it wakes the agent again when the situation changes. Because the policy remains a black box, TRIP wraps pretrained VLAs and WAMs without fine-tuning. We evaluate TRIP in simulation with three VLAs and one WAM on RoboHD, a benchmark of 168 scenes built by adding a reactive human avatar to 42 RoboCasa365 tasks~ nasiriany2026robocasa365 . RoboHD covers spatial, object-state, task-state, and perceptual disturbances, and any human-robot contact counts as failure. With the strongest policy, Xiaomi-Robotics-1, TRIP raises safety, the fraction of episodes without human contact among the scenes that can be solved without the person, from 61.3 to 81.3 relative to a turn-based harness using the same agent, action tools, and prompt, halving human contact. Task success is 38.7 versus 31.0 with the person and 73.2 versus 73.8 without, while agent invocations decrease from 30.3 to 19.4 per minute of robot time. TRIP is also safer than the turn-based harness with each of the other three policies. An ablation with Xiaomi-Robotics-1 shows that keeping the initial tripwire unchanged lowers safety to 61.3 . On two real-robot tasks, hanging a mug and hanging a towel, TRIP succeeds in 25 of 40 trials across two disturbance conditions (blocking the arm and moving the target object), compared with 5 of 40 for the turn-based harness and 1 of 40 for the policy alone. Our contributions are: TRIP, a training-free, policy-agnostic harness in which robot agents program their own interrupts: stateful tripwires that query a compact VLM during execution, compute on its answers, and are updated as the situation changes. RoboHD, a human-disturbance benchmark of 168 scenes built on 42 RoboCasa365 tasks, where any human-robot contact counts as failure. Experiments with three VLAs, one WAM, and a real robot: a matched comparison in which TRIP halves human contact with the strongest policy, an ablation on updating tripwires, and real-robot trials under disturbance. Related Work sec:related Robot foundation models and agentic manipulation. Recent advances in robot foundation models have enabled increasingly general manipulation capabilities. Vision-language-action (VLA) models learn transferable policies from large-scale robot data~ brohan2022rt,brohan2023rt,openx2024,kim2024openvla,octo2024,bousmalis2023robocat,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_,bjorck2025gr00t,team2026xiaomi , with diffusion-based architectures~ chi2023diffusion,liu2024rdt,zhao2023learning and multimodal conditioning~ jiang2022vima further expanding their capabilities. World action models extend this direction by jointly modeling actions and future observations~ ye2026world,wang2026action . Building on these pretrained models, language-model agents enable higher-level embodied reasoning~ driess2023palme,ahn2022can , program generation~ liang2023code,singh2023progprompt,huang2023voxposer , feedback-driven planning~ huang2022inner,rana2023sayplan,zha2023droc,liu2023reflect , and policy orchestration~ zhang2026harnessvla,chen2026showharness,wang2026auriga,team2026systematically . However, in turn-based agentic harnesses, the agent typically regains control only after a tool call returns, limiting its ability to respond to changes during execution. TRIP addresses this limitation by allowing the agent to interrupt ongoing policy execution without modifying the underlying policy. Runtime monitoring and event-driven control. Execution monitoring has been studied through language constraints, visual feedback, and generated programs~ guo2024doremi,zhou2025code,xu2025can . DoReMi~ guo2024doremi detects plan-execution misalignment through visual checks, while Code-as-Monitor~ zhou2025code evaluates generated spatiotemporal constraints. VoLo~ chen2026volo periodically monitors running policies with a VLM, and The Harness~ xu2026harness uses agent-written reactive guards. Event-triggered control similarly updates decisions when specified conditions hold~ tabuada2007event,heemels2012introduction . TRIP enables agents to write and revise stateful interruption programs that combine on-demand VLM perception with depth, geometry, and temporal memory, determining when to return control to the agent. title: NavTTT: Adaptive Parametric Memory via Hierarchical Test-Time Training for Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) demands that agents accumulate and reason over streaming visual observations throughout long navigation episodes. Existing approaches struggle to maintain long-term history, constrained by the finite context capacity of transformer architectures. To solve the problem, fast-weight test-time training (TTT) provides a mechanism for encoding streaming observations into an evolving parameter state. However, existing TTT does not distinguish informative observations from repetitive visual content, allowing redundant tokens to interfere with the retention of information needed for subsequent decisions. We propose Navigation-Conditioned Test-Time Training (NavTTT), which introduces adaptive memory formation and hierarchical memory integration for vision-and-language navigation. NavTTT leverages global navigation context to prioritize informative visual evidence and integrates language instructions with spatial information to construct spatially grounded memory representations. Episode-local nonlinear fast weights store these representations as Adaptive Parametric Memory (APM), preserving history beyond the visual context for later decisions. To reduce cross-layer coupling in memory formation, NavTTT maintains independent fast-weight memories across multiple decoder depths. This decoupled design prevents errors or biases from spreading across different memory levels. Meanwhile, it enables shared historical information to be independently represented at various levels of abstraction. Experiments demonstrate strong navigation performance on VLN-CE benchmarks and effective instruction following on a real robot.
