Introduction sec:intro Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) vln,vlnce requires an embodied agent to interpret natural-language instructions and sequentially interact with complex visual environments to reach a target destination. Unlike static vision-language understanding, navigation decisions are inherently history-dependent vlnbert : the agent must continuously relate its current observation to previously visited locations, encountered landmarks, and completed sub-goals in order to infer its progress and determine the next action hamt . This makes memory a fundamental component of VLN systems. An effective navigation memory should not only preserve useful historical information over long trajectories, but also selectively retain observations that remain relevant to future decisions memoir , while avoiding excessive accumulation of repetitive visual content janusvln . Existing VLN methods maintain navigation history through either explicit hamt,duet,etpnav or implicit memory vlnbert,krantz2023iterative,janusvln . Explicit memory organizes past experience into structured representations, such as maps, graphs, or trajectories, making historical state directly accessible to the agent. Implicit memory instead compresses history into latent representations, typically as recurrent features or persistent tokens propagated across time. While less structured, these implicit memories remain fundamentally token-based: retaining more history still requires preserving, updating, or repeatedly attending to an expanding set of latent states. This dependence becomes increasingly problematic in long-horizon navigation, where successive observations are highly redundant and only a small fraction of past information may remain relevant to future decisions. As a result, token-based memory must continuously balance historical coverage against a finite representational and computational budget. This limitation motivates a different form of implicit memory, where past experience is stored in the model state rather than kept as persistent representations, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser . Test-time training (TTT) sun2020ttt,sun2025ttt provides a mechanism for doing so by updating fast weights with incoming observations, allowing past information to persist in the model parameters titans . However, applying TTT directly to VLN is not straightforward. Navigation observations are highly redundant: nearby steps often produce similar visual inputs, while only a few observations remain useful for later decisions. Which observations matter also depends on the instruction, the agent's current location, and its progress along the route. Simply writing every observation into fast weights can therefore fill the memory with repeated or short-lived visual information and make important landmarks harder to preserve. In addition, navigation history needs to support different stages of decision making, while a generic fast-weight memory does not specify how historical information should be used across the navigation model. TTT-based memory for VLN therefore needs to address two key questions: what information should be stored, and how should that information be used during navigation. To address these challenges, we introduce Navigation-Conditioned Test-Time Training (NavTTT), a parametric memory framework that selectively internalizes navigation experience into episode-specific fast weights. NavTTT conditions memory formation on global navigation context, prioritizing visual evidence relevant to the instruction and navigation state while suppressing redundant content. It further integrates linguistic and spatial cues into the selected evidence, grounding memory in visual appearance and navigation context. To make accumulated experience accessible at multiple stages of navigation reasoning, NavTTT maintains independent fast-weight memories across decoder depths. Each memory transforms the selected evidence through its own association encoders and accumulates it via separate online updates. During subsequent decisions, hidden representations at each depth query the associated memory, integrating historical information with ongoing decoder computation. Together, adaptive memory formation and hierarchical memory integration allow navigation history to persist beyond limited visual context and inform subsequent decisions through layer-specific encoding and retrieval. We evaluate NavTTT on the R2R-CE vln and RxR-CE ku2020 benchmarks to examine the effectiveness of adaptive parametric memory for vision-and-language navigation. NavTTT achieves 66.7 SR and 59.4 SPL on R2R-CE, and 63.6 SR and 52.7 SPL on RxR-CE, consistently outperforming representative VLN baselines. Controlled ablations demonstrate that persistent fast-weight memory, online episode-level adaptation, and adaptive evidence selection each contribute substantially to navigation performance. Together, these results show that selectively internalizing navigation history through fast-weight updates provides an effective mechanism for preserving and exploiting long-horizon experience beyond the active visual context. We introduce NavTTT, a parametric memory framework for vision-and-language navigation that internalizes observations into episode-specific fast weights through test-time training, making accumulated experience accessible beyond the explicit visual context. We propose navigation-conditioned memory formation that jointly considers task relevance and visual redundancy when selecting evidence, and incorporates linguistic and spatial cues to construct grounded representations for memory updates. We develop a hierarchical memory architecture that independently encodes and accumulates shared historical evidence across decoder depths. Layer-specific queries retrieve this information during subsequent decisions, integrating persistent memory into multiple stages of navigation reasoning. Related Work sec:formatting Vision-Language Navigation and Memory Vision-language navigation (VLN) has evolved from vision-language pre-training and sequential history modeling toward foundation-model-based navigation. Early approaches leverage large-scale pre-training prevalent or explicitly model navigation history, such as recurrent state propagation in VLN-BERT vlnbert and long-horizon trajectory encoding in HAMT hamt . DUET duet further constructs an online topological map to couple global planning with local grounding. More recently, NavGPT navgpt and NaviLLM navillm explore LLM-based navigation reasoning, while NaVid navid , Uni-NaVid uninavid , and NaVILA navila extend VLMs toward end-to-end, unified, and real-world navigation. Our work complements this line by focusing specifically on how historical observations are retained and exploited during navigation. Recent VLN systems have consequently developed increasingly sophisticated memory mechanisms. StreamVLN streamvln maintains a slow-updating compressed visual context alongside a fast streaming context, while NavMorph navmorph introduces contextual evolution memory within a self-evolving world model. JanusVLN janusvln maintains separate spatial-geometric and visual-semantic histories as compact implicit memories, whereas HiMemVLN himemvln organizes navigation history through a hierarchical memory system. Memoir memoir further studies retrieval of accumulated environmental and behavioral experience across navigation episodes. Unlike these approaches, NavTTT selectively writes navigation-relevant observations into online-adapted fast weights, treating the model parameters themselves as persistent memory during an episode. Parametric Memory and Test-Time Training Test-time training (TTT) was originally introduced for self-supervised adaptation on unlabeled test samples sun2020ttt , but has recently been repurposed as a sequence-modeling mechanism in which fast weights serve as recurrent state sun2025ttt . This view is closely related to earlier fast-weight formulations of linear attention: schlag2021linear interpret linear Transformers as fast-weight programmers that store key--value associations in rapidly changing weights. Modern TTT generalizes this perspective by allowing a learnable, potentially nonlinear model to serve as the evolving parameter state. Titans titans develops such online neural memory for long-context modeling, while LaCT tttdoneright enables large nonlinear fast-weight states through efficient large-chunk updates. Recent work further explores fast weights as explicit parametric memory for adaptive inference and agents. title: Trailblazer-F: Speculative Action-Flow Inference for Autonomous Driving
summary: Driving world-action models generate planned trajectories through iterative action denoising, with each update depending on the preceding state. This sequential dependency incurs substantial inference latency, limiting timely planning. Speculative inference offers an opportunity to reduce this latency by predicting future denoising states for parallel target evaluation, but requires efficient proposal generation and suitable verification for continuous actions. We present Trailblazer-F, a speculative action-flow inference framework in which a lightweight drafter acts as a trailblazer, charting a candidate denoising path through the compact, structured waypoint space so that the target model can verify multiple steps in parallel and advance with fewer sequential updates. Our method maintains planning quality while keeping the pretrained target model frozen.Across all 12,146 NAVSIM v1 navtest scenes, Trailblazer-F maintains near-baseline planning performance, with PDMS changes of +0.04 and -0.08 points for SimWAM and DriveWAM, respectively. Paired inference measurements on an NVIDIA L20 GPU yield 2.31x and 1.55x speedups. Flow matching has become widely adopted in recent vision-based world-action models for learning visual dynamics and continuous driving actions~ zhou2026drivedreamerpolicy,shi2026drivewam,zhao2026simwam,wang2026svwam,parikh2026physwam . However, standard sampling introduces a sequential bottleneck: each denoising update requires a target-model evaluation conditioned on the preceding state, as shown in Fig.~ fig:introduction (a)~ lipman2023flow,shi2026drivewam,wang2026svwam . Our profiling shows that action denoising accounts for most inference latency in the evaluated models. This overhead conflicts with the need for timely planning in dynamic traffic~ jiang2023vad,liao2025diffusiondrive . Reducing the cost of action denoising while preserving planning quality is therefore a key challenge in bringing world models to real-time autonomous driving. Existing efforts to accelerate generative inference include distilling multi-step samplers into fewer-step generators~ salimans2022progressive , learning truncated denoising processes for driving policies~ liao2025diffusiondrive , and designing action branches that avoid future-video generation at inference~ zhao2026simwam,wang2026svwam . These approaches improve efficiency by modifying the model architecture or changing the sampling dynamics, which can alter the generator's output distribution. Consequently, the planning behavior of the original pretrained model is not necessarily preserved. This motivates a complementary objective: accelerating action-flow inference while keeping the pretrained target model's parameters and architecture unchanged and preserving its planning quality. Speculative decoding offers a promising approach to this objective: a lightweight drafter proposes multiple candidates for parallel target verification, reducing sequential evaluations while retaining the pretrained target~ leviathan2023speculative,chen2023speculative,li2024eagle . Despite progress in diffusion and flow generation~ debortoli2025speculative,bajpai2026flowcast , applying this paradigm to world models for autonomous driving requires overcoming two key challenges. First, inexpensive multi-step state prediction: future denoising states depend on successive target updates, making it difficult for a lightweight drafter to predict several states accurately without reproducing the costly sequential computation. Second, reliable continuous-state verification: exact matching is too restrictive for continuous states, whereas accepting inaccurate proposals can degrade planning quality. An effective verifier must therefore distinguish useful approximations from unacceptable deviations from the target dynamics. By unfolding the ten-step action-flow denoising process in SimWAM and DriveWAM and inspecting its intermediate states, we observe two properties that help address these challenges. First, a compact waypoint representation: each state contains eight waypoints with position and heading coordinates, forming an representation throughout denoising~ zhao2026simwam,shi2026drivewam . This low-dimensional structure motivates lightweight prediction of multiple future denoising states. Second, consistent physical semantics: the state coordinates remain associated with waypoint positions and headings across denoising steps, even when intermediate states are noisy~ shi2026drivewam,zhou2026drivedreamerpolicy,wang2026svwam . A candidate state and its target correction at the same denoising time can therefore be compared waypoint by waypoint through aligned position and heading channels in a common normalized coordinate system. This correspondence provides an interpretable basis for tolerance-based verification against the target dynamics. Motivated by these challenges and observations, we propose Trailblazer-F, a speculative inference framework tailored to action flow in autonomous-driving world models. Like a pathfinder scouting the route ahead, a lightweight drafter anticipates future denoising states, allowing the target model to verify multiple proposals in parallel. The drafter exploits the compact action representation to predict span-specific endpoints in a single forward pass, then constructs future states analytically using the known noise schedule. For verification, the target independently computes solver-aligned, one-step corrections from the corresponding proposed predecessor states. Each candidate must satisfy a normalized discrepancy threshold at every waypoint, and only the consecutive passing prefix is accepted. Together, these designs exploit the structure of action flow to reduce sequential inference latency while controlling local deviations from the target dynamics, as shown in Fig.~ fig:introduction (b). We develop three complementary components: a lightweight action-flow drafter for multi-step state prediction, state-based parallel verification that independently generates solver-aligned target corrections, and a physically interpretable acceptance mechanism that checks normalized position and heading consistency at every waypoint. We evaluate Trailblazer-F on all 12,146 NAVSIM v1 navtest scenes across two world-action models, maintaining near-baseline planning scores while achieving up to inference speedup on an NVIDIA L20 GPU. Real-vehicle experiments on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin further demonstrate onboard acceleration and qualitative trajectory agreement with native sampling. Related Work sec:related Driving world-action models. Driving world-action models (WAMs) connect future-scene prediction with ego-motion generation, transferring generative world representations into driving policies. Epona~ zhang2025epona employs rectified flow for both next-frame and trajectory generation, conditioned on shared spatiotemporal features. DriveVA~ liu2026driveva jointly generates future video latents and action tokens through a shared flow-matching decoder, strengthening the connection between imagined scene evolution and planned motion. DriveWAM~ shi2026drivewam similarly adapts pretrained video generative priors to an autoregressive video-action policy with a joint flow-matching objective. Complementary designs introduce specialized experts or additional geometric supervision. SimWAM~ zhao2026simwam co-trains video and action experts through joint flow matching, while isolating their attention so that action inference does not require future-video generation. DriveDreamer-Policy~ zhou2026drivedreamerpolicy incorporates geometry-aware conditioning through modular depth, video, and action generators. More directly within WAMs, OSWAM~ zhang2026oswam enables one-step action generation through learned structured initialization and privileged-information distillation. Such designs can retain competitive planning performance, but require specialized training or changes to the action-generation architecture. Conversely, aggressive step reduction without corresponding adaptation can degrade planning quality, as illustrated by the one-step baselines reported in OSWAM~ zhang2026oswam . Speculative inference offers a complementary approach based on target verification. Following speculative decoding~ leviathan2023speculative , De Bortoli et al.~ debortoli2025speculative preserve target distributions for stochastic diffusion chains, but their procedure does not directly apply to deterministic samplers. FlowCast~ bajpai2026flowcast uses velocity extrapolation and parallel error-based verification for visual generation. Closely related, Realtime-VLA FLASH~ niu2026realtimevlaflash drafts action chunks, reuses context across replanning rounds, and checks the consistency of reconstructed endpoints to select executable action prefixes. Acceptance advances along denoising steps rather than action execution, retaining the target architecture, parameters, and sampling schedule. As illustrates, action denoising follows a progressive refinement process, with waypoint positions gradually approaching the final trajectory. title: AELF: Active Terrain-Aware UAV Exploration Using a Lightweight Framework
summary: This paper presents an efficient and robust approach for autonomous aerial exploration in complex environments. Instead of relying on conventional 3D voxel-based maps for exploration, we utilize a lightweight 2.5D map framework that reduces computational overhead while preserving essential topographic information. More importantly, this representation systematically eliminates the blind voxel problem commonly encountered in voxel-based exploration due to occlusions and limited visibility. Unlike previous methods that rely on a fixed altitude scale for exploration, our approach requires no prior height information and actively adapts to terrain elevation changes during exploration. To further enhance exploration efficiency while preserving the generality of 3D exploration, we perform 2D path planning on the 2.5D map framework, which is then lifted to 3D to evaluate the cost between viewpoints by taking into account terrain traversability, thereby reducing frequent altitude changes and enabling smoother exploration. Extensive experiments conducted in both simulated and real-world environments demonstrate the effectiveness and advantages of our approach over existing solutions. Our approach demonstrates fast exploration of over 2000~$\text{m}^2$ of cluttered forest and sloped mountainous terrain with elevation changes of up to 10~m, reaching a maximum speed of 5~m/s in real-world tests.

Autonomous Aerial Systems, Exploration, Coverage Planning, Terrain awareness, Search and Rescue Introduction n real-world applications such as search and rescue, environmental monitoring, infrastructure inspection, and space exploration, autonomous exploration plays a critical role. These tasks often involve complex terrains—flat areas, slopes, and rugged regions—where robots equipped with advanced sensors can map environments and detect obstacles in real time. In time-sensitive scenarios like disaster response, precise geometric reconstruction is often unnecessary; what matters more is the rapid acquisition of traversable 3D structures to support fast decision-making. Many of these missions rely on multi-robot collaboration, where aerial robots provide quick scene coverage despite limited endurance. Efficient use of their capabilities offers valuable environmental priors for planning and deploying ground-based systems. Several existing methods focus on autonomous exploration in 2D environments and have achieved promising results in flat or structured terrains yamauchi1997frontier, ExplorDRL2019, li2025daptp, hu2020voronoi . However, they perform poorly in environments with unstructured topography, such as hills or sloped terrain. In such cases, 2D exploration techniques fail to capture vertical structure, often resulting in incomplete map coverage and inefficient navigation. Moreover, relying solely on 2D sensors limits the robot’s ability to accurately distinguish between traversable and non-traversable areas in three-dimensional space, potentially compromising safety in real-world deployments cao2024hma . These limitations reduce overall exploration effectiveness and hinder reliable operation in rugged or uneven environments, highlighting the need for more advanced strategies capable of handling 3D spatial complexity. To address this, modern systems increasingly use 3D sensors such as LiDARs and RGB-D cameras cao2021tare, zhou2024oto, lu2024fapp . These sensors offer richer spatial information than 2D ones: LiDAR produces accurate geometric point clouds, while RGB-D cameras offer both geometric and texture cues, enabling more informed decision-making in visually complex spaces. Most existing 3D exploration methods model the environment using occupancy grid maps with predefined resolutions and height limits. The aim is to estimate the occupancy state of each grid cell during navigation, and the exploration size is preset to ensure that the unknown occupancy grid fully encloses the target regions. However, without prior knowledge of the environment’s geometry, such preset height constraints can lead to high memory usage or missed regions, reducing exploration accuracy and completeness. In 3D exploration, some methods improve efficiency by discarding clusters with few frontiers or those deemed unreachable zhou2021fuel, zhou2023racer, luperto2024estimating . This allows the robot to focus on more informative and accessible areas, enhancing planning efficiency. In contrast, other approaches zhou2024oto, bartolomei2023fast do not ignore smaller or marginal unexplored regions. Instead, they incorporate these areas into the planning process, aiming to clear space more systematically rather than exclusively prioritizing regions with the highest expected information gain. While such methods are applicable to 3D environments, they are typically designed for scenarios with relatively structured spatial layouts zhao2023autonomous . In environments with complex and unstructured obstacles, such as forests, cluster reachability is often assessed during execution rather than prior to planning. This reactive checking can lead to inefficiencies, such as wasted planning cycles or idle waiting for unreachable clusters to be cleared, thereby disrupting exploration continuity. Although 2D maps offer substantial advantages over 3D voxel grids in terms of reduced memory usage and computational load, effective conversion from 3D to 2D remains challenging. The most common approach projects the 3D voxel map, such as OctoMap hornung2013octomap , onto a 2D plane. A more advanced method, HMAPs yang2018efficient , supports conversion from 3D to both 2.5D and 2D maps via downward projection. However, these projection-based techniques have inherent limitations. For example, any obstacle on the ground or ceiling is also projected onto the 2D map, potentially causing ambiguity in occupancy interpretation. Additionally, any structure outside the projection range is omitted entirely, causing incomplete environment representation. These drawbacks limit the generalization of such methods in environments with rich vertical structures or overhanging elements. To address the limitations mentioned above, especially in complex environments with significant terrain variation and unknown scale, we propose AELF (Active Exploration using a Lightweight Framework). In this framework, 3D frontiers are extracted from a 2D grid map, and their corresponding elevations are retrieved from a height map. Regions that lack sufficient traversable space are filtered out using a predefined safety threshold to ensure safe and feasible planning. By utilizing spatial information, we estimate local terrain slopes to evaluate the terrain traversability. This enables the integration of terrain-aware cost terms into the planning process, which encourages smoother and more consistent exploration trajectories. Our main contributions are as follows: A projection-free method is used to convert 3D maps into 2D representations by extracting free space directly, enabling robust exploration in complex and unstructured outdoor environments. Terrain elevation is adaptively corrected using a sensor-aware model to prevent height bootstrapping during exploration. A 2.5D map framework is used for frontier detection and 3D path generation to accelerate exploration planning. This design systematically eliminates the blind voxel problem commonly encountered in outdoor exploration. By considering traversability information, the system retains 3D exploration generality while using 2D terrain cues for smoother motion and fewer altitude changes. Extensive simulations and real-world experiments validate the framework, with the system running on a self-built UAV and tested in challenging forest exploration at speeds up to 5 m/s, as shown in Fig. fig: cover . Related work Map Representation for Autonomous Systems Maps play a fundamental role in autonomous systems such as UAVs and ground vehicles, enabling key functionalities like localization, motion planning, and obstacle avoidance. Among various map representations, 2D and 3D metric grid maps are the most widely adopted due to their simplicity and compatibility with common algorithms. While 3D maps offer detailed spatial representation, 2D maps are more efficient in terms of computation and memory. Combining both is often advantageous, but maintaining separate 2D and 3D mapping pipelines, such as by projecting 3D data onto a 2D plane or using different sensors to generate separate maps, increases system complexity and may lead to inconsistencies that degrade planning accuracy and robustness Fred2024voxel . To address this, unified mapping frameworks for autonomous platforms aim to generate maps directly from raw sensor data. Prior studies have converted point clouds into 2D maps tao2024mobile, chen2024lidar or extracted elevation values as 2D height images wang2025terrain . However, these often struggle with vertical structures such as overhangs and ceilings, leading to incomplete or distorted maps. Projection-based methods, such as filtering out floor points before projection li2023advanced , are usually sensor-specific and less generalizable across different autonomous systems. Translating 3D voxel maps into 2D representations remains relatively underexplored, especially for UAVs operating in large-scale, unstructured environments. A common method is to project a fixed-height slice onto a 2D plane, as in OctoMap hornung2013octomap . SkiMap de2017skimap improves efficiency by classifying voxels and updating a specific SkipList Tree layer. However, such projections inherently discard vertical information, misrepresenting environments with elevation variation. They may misinterpret ground or ceiling voxels and fail to detect obstacles beyond a fixed height range. While such limitations are often acceptable in flat indoor environments, they can pose significant challenges in large-scale outdoor scenarios. To address this, we utilize a lightweight, task-oriented mapping framework for autonomous exploration. Our method merges the efficiency of 2D frontier detection with the 3D spatial fidelity, enabling effective exploration in environments with complex elevation changes. title: ViewDreamer: A Robot World Model beyond Fixed Camera Setups
summary: Video generation models are increasingly important for robot learning, yet most generate each camera view separately or tile all views in a fixed layout. Robot demonstrations, however, are captured by synchronized cameras whose number, placement, and order vary across embodiments. We present ViewDreamer, a single world model that handles variable sets of cameras by disentangling per-view generation from cross-view interaction. Each view follows the generation path of a pretrained single-view model, and views interact only through shared slot tokens. We stabilize multi-view training with a curriculum that gradually increases the number of views. Cross-View Slot Agreement uses visual foundation models to group geometrically and semantically similar regions across views into shared slots. On RoboView-Bench, which covers one to four cameras, ViewDreamer achieves the best generation quality among the models evaluated and improves cross-view consistency over independent per-view generation. These gains carry over to our world-action model (WAM) and action-conditioned world model (AC-WM). Our WAM outperforms the FastWAM-Joint baseline on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboDojo, and on a real Franka robot. Both variants improve out-of-domain generalization to various camera settings and scenes.
full_text: Introduction section:intro Video generation models are increasingly used in robot learning. They can synthesize training data~ jang2025dreamgen,liu2025robotransfer , evaluate policies without physical deployment~ zhu2024irasim,guo2025ctrlworld , and serve as policy backbones~ wu2024gr1,ye2026dreamzero,yuan2026fastwam . Robots usually record a task with several synchronized cameras from complementary viewpoints. An embodied world model should predict what every camera will see, and these predictions must agree wherever views overlap. We call this property cross-view consistency. =-1 Most video generation models, however, produce one video from one image~ blattmann2023videoldm,wan2025 . A common workaround tiles all views into one grid~ nvidia2026cosmos3,ye2026dreamzero,liu2025robotransfer . Tiling trades resolution against compute. A grid at the pretrained resolution shrinks each view, whereas an enlarged grid makes the computational cost of attention grow quadratically with the view count. Tiling also ties each camera to a fixed grid position and places the views side by side, a layout rare in single-camera pretraining videos. Other approaches attend across views or condition on camera geometry yet assume a fixed camera rig~ liao2025genieenvisioner,guo2025ctrlworld,huang2025enerverse,jiang2025evac,paiworld2026 . Real camera setups differ in number, placement, and order from robot to robot, and even between datasets of one robot. Bimanual robots typically carry more wrist cameras than single-arm robots, and humanoids carry more cameras than fixed arms~ khazatsky2024droid,agibotworld2025,jiang2025galaxea,wu2025robocoin . Embodied world models therefore need a video backbone that stays cross-view consistent across such camera setups. =-1 Our key idea is to disentangle per-view generation from cross-view interaction. A pretrained video generator models single-view appearance and motion, yet cannot keep multiple views consistent. We therefore process every view with the same pretrained backbone. Views communicate only through shared slots, which are learnable vectors that gather related regions from all views. We train the whole model jointly. The model retains per-view quality and accepts a variable number of views in any order at a computational cost linear in the view count. Without supervision, the slots tend to merge similar patches across views, such as those of one object, yet the grouping stays fragmented. We show that supervising this grouping improves cross-view consistency. implements this design with three components (Fig.~ fig:method-overview ). After every block of a pretrained video diffusion transformer, a Cross-View Interaction (CVI) module exchanges information among all views through the slots. Each CVI module starts as an identity mapping, and a View-Count Curriculum (VCC) begins with single views and adds more. The model thus grows from the pretrained single-view generator into a multi-view one. Cross-View Slot Agreement (CSA) provides this supervision by distilling region relations from frozen visual foundation models into the slot assignments. We train on 2.99M clips, including real-robot recordings from 14 embodiments, and build from 500 held-out four-camera episodes. On with three and four views, leads all compared generators in fidelity and improves cross-view consistency over independent per-view generation. In a controlled ablation, every component improves policy success and nearly all generation metrics. Better prediction thus appears to help control. CVI also produces better videos than full cross-view attention at a lower computational cost. As an action-conditioned world model, scores highest among the compared models in both clean and randomized scenes. Our policies add CVI to FastWAM-Joint~ yuan2026fastwam and are initialized from . They outperform the original FastWAM-Joint in simulation with two or three cameras and on a real Franka robot. In simulation, these gains are largest in out-of-domain (OOD) settings, such as unseen scenes, new camera viewpoints, or sensor noise. Our contributions are: [leftmargin=1.25em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt] : a robot world model that predicts cross-view-consistent future videos for a variable number of cameras. It disentangles per-view generation on the pretrained single-view path from cross-view interaction through shared slot tokens. Cross-View Slot Agreement: a training-time alignment objective that makes geometrically and semantically similar regions in different views share a slot. A View-Count Curriculum complements it by growing the model from single-view to multi-view generation. title: Real-Time On-Drone Hyperspectral Anomaly Detection for Wilderness Search and Rescue
summary: Wilderness search-and-rescue (WSAR) teams use uncrewed aerial systems (UASs) to survey terrain for indicators of missing persons that are rare, blend into the background, or lack thermal signatures. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) provides rich spectral information, but its high data volume challenges real-time on-drone processing. We present SABL, an edge-computing pipeline for on-drone Spectral Anomaly-Based Localization. SABL integrates hyperspectral streaming with exponentially moving Reed-Xiaoli (ERX) anomaly detection and DBSCAN spatial filtering to group pixel-level anomalies into candidate search regions. SABL is evaluated on data collected during a 10-day deployment with Quinhagak Search and Rescue (QSAR) in remote Alaska. It processes hyperspectral scanlines at 5.67-5.73 ms per line, meeting the camera's 10-ms acquisition interval; DBSCAN requires only 6.5-12.5 ms per 100-line update for filtering. SABL achieves approximately 56% and 99% object-level precision on QSAR-selected search indicators across two scenes, with corresponding recall of 55% and 29%, providing significant background filtering while identifying difficult-to-see anomalous search indicators.
full_text: Real-Time On-Drone Hyperspectral Anomaly Detection for Wilderness Search and Rescue Jacqueline Liu, Gyabaah Kyere, Chengyan Liu, Kenneth Chiu, Lynn Marie (Kic'i) Church, Sean Gleason, and Jayson Boubin Wilderness search-and-rescue (WSAR) teams use uncrewed aerial systems (UASs) to survey terrain for indicators of missing persons that are rare, blend into the background, or lack thermal signatures. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) provides rich spectral information, but its high data volume challenges real-time on-drone processing. We present SABL, an edge-computing pipeline for on-drone Spectral Anomaly-Based Localization. SABL integrates hyperspectral streaming with exponentially moving Reed–Xiaoli (ERX) anomaly detection and DBSCAN spatial filtering to group pixel-level anomalies into candidate search regions. SABL is evaluated on data collected during a 10-day deployment with Quinhagak Search and Rescue (QSAR) in remote Alaska. It processes hyperspectral scanlines at 5.67-5.73 ms per line, meeting the camera’s 10-ms acquisition interval; DBSCAN requires only 6.5-12.5 ms per 100-line update for filtering. SABL achieves approximately 56 and 99 object-level precision on QSAR-selected search indicators across two scenes, with corresponding recall of 55 and 29 , providing significant background filtering while identifying difficult-to-see anomalous search indicators. Wilderness Search and Rescue (WSAR), Real-Time Hyperspectral Anomaly Detection, Uncrewed Aerial Systems (UASs). Introduction ilderness Search and Rescue (WSAR) operations require teams of trained operators to locate indicators of missing persons, including man-made objects, tracks, and the persons themselves, across vast areas that can be difficult to access. Uncrewed aerial systems (UASs) offer a fast, maneuverable, and relatively inexpensive way to sense these environments, helping WSAR teams inspect terrain and identify locations that warrant closer investigation. Consequently, UASs have attracted growing interest among WSAR teams, with existing work exploring their integration into WSAR workflows and the use of visual and thermal sensing for indicator detection~ drones4030038, schedl_2020, BroylesHaynerEtAl2022, UAV_WSAR . However, collecting aerial imagery is only part of the problem. WSAR teams must also determine where potentially relevant objects appear in the imagery, often under challenging environmental conditions and within time-sensitive operations. A typical WSAR workflow involves both aerial and terrestrial search. WSAR teams commonly use crewed and uncrewed aircraft to collect conventional visible (EO/RGB) and infrared (IR) imagery. RGB imagery provides intuitive situational awareness, while IR imagery can identify heat signatures indicative of human presence, or of humans themselves schedl_2020, BroylesHaynerEtAl2022 . In vast, remote areas where WSAR operations usually take place, UAS imagery helps ground teams execute search grids faster, extend awareness into hazardous terrain, and locate possible evacuation routes for critical patients drones4030038, BroylesHaynerEtAl2022 . These capabilities can reduce search time and improve responder safety. RGB and IR imagery, however, have significant limitations. RGB imagery suffers from many of the same factors that challenge human vision: search environments are often cluttered, contain repetitive patterns that humans readily filter out, and may include brush or tree canopies that partially occludes objects that would otherwise be recognizable by shape liu2026rtrx . Furthermore, missing persons may also wear camouflage, or earth-toned clothing that is difficult to distinguish from natural backgrounds in high-altitude aerial imagery (Figure fig:system_design ). IR imagery complements RGB sensing by measuring emitted thermal radiation, but cannot reliably identify materials that indicate human presence without a strong heat signature, such as tents, tarps, or discarded clothing. It may also fail to detect missing persons wearing insulated clothing, or deceased individuals~ BroylesHaynerEtAl2022 (Figure fig:rgb-ir ). Neither modality provides a direct way to differentiate anomalous materials that are partially occluded, deliberately camouflaged, insulated, or lacking a conventional thermal signature. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) offers a complementary source of information. Unlike RGB cameras, which capture three broad spectral channels, hyperspectral cameras measure spectral radiance across many (typically 100+) narrow spectral bands (Figure fig:profile ). These measurements can expose material-composition differences that are not apparent in conventional imagery, making HSI promising for detecting anomalous materials and objects in complex scenes~ su2021hyperspectral, matteoli2010tutorial . This additional information comes at a computational cost. Hyperspectral sensors generate large data volumes, and many UAS-compatible systems use push-broom sensors that acquire imagery one line at a time. Pixel-wise inference on these high-dimensional streams requires substantial computation, and subsequent geometric correction and photogrammetry introduce significant additional latency~ gomez2008correction, ERX . State-of-the-practice workflows store imagery for post-flight processing on high-performance computing equipment. For time-sensitive WSAR operations, processing imagery as it is acquired can be as important as detecting anomalies accurately, because missing persons lost or injured may face hypothermia, hypovolemia, and shock if stranded. Onboard processing removes dependence on data offloading, thereby allowing potential indicators to be localized while a mission is underway. Achieving this capability, however, requires an integrated pipeline that can receive the sensor stream, decode hyperspectral measurements, and execute detection quickly enough to keep pace with acquisition on resource-constrained hardware. Hyperspectral anomaly detection (HAD) provides a promising starting point. HAD algorithms identify pixels that differ statistically from a sensed background distribution~ RX, ERX . HAD is a common workload across agriculture, defense, environmental monitoring, etc., but is rarely adapted to real-time processing~ goudemant2024onboard, shimoni2019hyperspectral, abdulsalam2024unsupervised . HAD techniques are generally evaluated on corrected and post-processed data, and often run on entire datasets to identify global anomalies~ RX . Recent improvements in on-drone processing power and hyperspectral camera miniaturization have increased interest in real-time HAD. Prior works have demonstrated real-time hyperspectral detection of specific environmental phenomena~ REMIX, spectramine , near-real time on-drone HAD~ watson2026real , and an algorithm suited to real-time HAD for push-broom HSI sensors~ ERX . In our earlier work, we introduced Real-Time Reed-Xiaoli (RT-RX), an edge computing pipeline that integrates real-time HSI streaming with real-time HAD~ liu2026rtrx . RT-RX demonstrates that HSI can be acquired and processed in real-time onboard a UAS, but its detection outputs are limited to pixel-level anomaly scores. In a WSAR scenario, this places the burden of interpreting and filtering noisy HAD outputs on the operators, which may cause them to overlook or misinterpret critical information during time-sensitive searches. In this work, we present Spectral Anomaly-Based Localization (SABL), an extension of RT-RX designed to generate interpretable outputs for WSAR operators (Figure fig:system_design ). SABL retains RT-RX's real-time hyperspectral streaming and line-based anomaly detection while adding spatial filtering via Density Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN)~ DBSCAN . DBSCAN suppresses isolated detections and retains dense anomaly regions for operator inspection instead of raw pixel-wise detections. To evaluate SABL, we worked with Quinhagak Search and Rescue (QSAR), a real WSAR team in remote Alaska, and conducted a 10-day data-collection campaign. We collected HSI of search-relevant objects in-situ, including clothing, fishing equipment, survival gear, and other objects which would immediately cue close inspection. We show that SABL processes hyperspectral data at 5.7 ms per line on a Raspberry Pi 4B, and achieves approximately 56 and 99 object-level precision on real WSAR search indicators across two realistic scenes. The main contributions of SABL are as follows: A real-time, on-drone hyperspectral edge-computing system for WSAR. SABL's processing pipeline comprises HSI streaming, line-based HAD, and spatial filtering to identify and localize WSAR search indicators. A field-collected hyperspectral dataset developed in collaboration with a real WSAR team in remote, rural Alaska. SABL provides a field-grounded evaluation for HAD in austere environment, with a data collection guided by a real WSAR team. A application-driven evaluation of system performance and detection capabilities. We evaluate SABL's processing throughput relative to the sensor acquisition rate and characterize pixel- and object-level detection performance across two field scenes with differing background complexity. Our evaluation identifies both the conditions under which SABL produces useful search indicators and the environmental factors continue to challenge reliable detection. Background sec:Background Search and Rescue in Remote Alaska Quinhagak, Alaska, lies along the Bering Sea coast in the Yukon–Kuskokwim Delta, amid a landscape of rivers, lakes, and permafrost. It is one of 56 Yup'ik villages off the road system in western Alaska where villagers rely on snow machines, small marine skiffs, barges, and Cessna-style airplanes for transportation and logistics. Like many communities across the circumpolar north, daily life is typified by an emphasis on subsistence hunting, fishing, and gathering, which can result in a high operational tempo for locally led rescue missions. For instance, a village may experience up to three SAR missions per week during peak summer months, when villagers are regularly traversing the tundra to hunt and gather food. Villages in the Yukon-Kuskokwim delta, due to their remoteness, generally manage their own SAR processes. Quinhagak Search and Rescue (QSAR), is a non-profit organization which trains and organizes volunteer responders from the local community. When an event occurs, QSAR is generally activated by tribal public safety officers, who collect information about the missing person using a Lost Person Behavior survey LPB . The survey documents the individual's intended travel plans, physical description (e.g., clothing, age, and vehicle type), and last known location to inform search strategies. Additionally, indigenous teachings, tracking skills, and understanding of their environment and human behavior form a traditional knowledge system that is central to QSAR. QSAR operators also use small quadrotor UASs equipped with EO/IR sensors to quickly inspect hazardous or difficult-to-reach areas (e.g., coastal mudflats; Figure fig:qsar ). Missing persons in Quinhagak generally wear insulated or camouflaged clothing, and carry earth-toned or camouflaged hunting and fishing equipment which often does not appear distinctly in EO/IR imagery (Figure fig:system_design ). We hypothesize that a system capable of real-time HAD could enable this detection capability. title: $γ$-Scape: An Agent-Centric World for Mobile Embodied Intelligence
summary: Recent embodied agents construct and adapt robot behavior through executable programs, tool use, and interaction feedback. Studying these systems in mobile manipulation calls for physical worlds that connect agent-directed execution with its physical consequences and reusable interaction experience. We introduce $γ$-Scape, an agent-centric simulation and benchmark platform for mobile embodied intelligence. Agents compose motion tools and learned skills to carry out complete tasks that combine navigation and manipulation in a persistent physical world. BenchForge grounds structured objectives in physical task instances with instructions, reference programs, and goal evaluators, defining task goals while preserving agents' choice of valid solutions. An agentic collection harness further enables agents to produce demonstrations by carrying out contact-rich interactions through sustained control and physical feedback. Assisted reference execution and human guidance provide complementary experience. The resulting tool traces and aligned observation-action records support program refinement and policy learning, with common task-goal criteria for subsequent evaluation. We benchmark representative agent systems on complete tasks and demonstrate contact collection and trace-informed program revision. Together, these workflows provide infrastructure for research on embodied recursive self-improvement.
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction Recent advances in embodied agents have broadened how robot behavior is constructed and adapted. Agents generate executable programs over perception and control interfaces~ codeaspolicies,capx , use execution feedback to revise programs and retain reusable skills~ aspire,rax , and combine learned action skills with analytic motion tools~ harnessvla . Mobile agents use multimodal observations and action interfaces to pursue goals across multiple locations~ owmm . In mobile manipulation, each action changes the conditions for the next. Opening a cabinet changes access, grasping occupies a hand, and transport changes the conditions for placement. To retrieve supplies from storage and deliver them elsewhere, an agent must coordinate these interactions and respond to their measured outcomes. Existing activity benchmarks and generative environments provide valuable tasks and demonstration resources~ behavior1k,manitaskgen,robocasa365 . We ask how a physical world can support complete-task evaluation while retaining the interaction context needed to construct and revise behavior. We introduce , an agent-centric simulation and benchmark platform for complete mobile manipulation tasks ( ). The platform combines 370 indoor scenes with 11,073 interactive object assets for task construction. Task agents compose their own programs and tool calls, combining motion tools and learned skills according to the states reached during execution. BenchForge turns structured task requirements into physical instances by binding resources, constructing connected layouts, and applying geometric and physical checks. Each instance includes an instruction, a reference program, and a goal evaluator. The reference program supports construction and collection, while the evaluator checks requested outcomes and process conditions. This separation lets researchers compare agent-chosen solutions under a fixed task definition and retain the same goals when revising behavior. Different embodiments and shared-space participants provide additional physical contexts for studying these behaviors. also supports agents as producers of experience for behavior development. In this complementary workflow, native planning handles routine motion while a dedicated collection agent uses privileged physical feedback to control contact interactions. It retains control through extraction, release, and withdrawal before task execution resumes from the measured state. Each interaction yields both tool traces for program refinement and aligned robot observations and actions for skill adaptation. Assisted reference execution and human guidance provide complementary demonstrations with explicit control-source and assistance labels. The execution interfaces accept revised programs and learned skills for further runs under unchanged task goals, providing infrastructure for research on embodied recursive self-improvement. We construct a fixed benchmark of 22 task families and 220 task instances spanning delivery, organization, storage and access, preparation and restoration, and carrying and coordination. We compare representative agent systems as integrated into the platform, using common physical instances and task-goal criteria while retaining each system's reasoning and execution interfaces. Complete-task success measures the requested outcome, while semantic progress records accumulated intermediate accomplishment. Our experiments connect these results to execution traces and show how a failed contact interaction informs an executed program revision. Our contributions are threefold: =10000 A world for agent-directed mobile manipulation. We combine task-driven physical construction with composable execution interfaces, allowing agents to pursue explicit goals through programs, motion tools, and learned skills grounded in measured physical outcomes. Experience production for behavior development. We provide sustained agentic contact collection within complete tasks, alongside assisted and human-guided experience. We demonstrate contact collection and trace-informed program revision, retaining tool feedback and temporally aligned observation--action records for further adaptation. A benchmark of complete embodied agent systems. We construct a 22-family, 220-instance suite and examine representative systems through complete-task success, semantic progress, and physical execution analysis. Code as Policies~ codeaspolicies represents behavior through programs over perception and control interfaces, while CaP-X~ capx studies coding agents through interface abstractions and execution feedback. ASPIRE~ aspire and RAX~ rax develop reusable behavior through program refinement and online exploration, respectively. Harness VLA~ harnessvla combines a frozen vision-language-action model with analytic primitives and execution memory. Mobile systems such as HomeRobot~ homerobot , BUMBLE~ bumble , and OWMM-Agent~ owmm integrate perception, reasoning, and action interfaces for tasks spanning multiple locations. Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) studies instruction following in visual environments, spanning individual navigation and multi-robot coordination~ navid,uninavid,spacevln,conavbench,deconav,cogddn,sparsevideonav,compass1,sagenav,navform,qwenrobotnav . For learned navigation, WNM-3D~ wnm3d conditions joint future-view and navigation-action generation on 3D scene representations. complements these architectures with grounded tasks and a runtime for executing agent-chosen behavior under common goal criteria. Interactive worlds and embodied benchmarks. ALFRED~ alfred , Habitat 2.0~ habitat2 , and BEHAVIOR-1K~ behavior1k provide settings for instruction following, rearrangement, and everyday physical activities. summary: Vision-Language Navigation(VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow language instructions through unseen 3D environments, where the target spaces often lie beyond the current observation. Navigation world models address this challenge by predicting future views either as pixels or latent representations, providing valuable look-ahead information for action decision. Both paradigms define the future primarily through what the agent may observe, raising a fundamental question: is predicting future views the ultimate form to represent the future for VLN? Cognitive studies show that the human hippocampus prospectively represents both future goals and intervening locations along planned routes. Inspired by this predictive-map view, we organize the navigation-relevant future around goal-directed spatial states and route structure. We instantiate this perspective with two complementary abstractions: a short-horizon waypoint that specifies the next local state to reach, and a mid-horizon corridor that captures the spatial support of the upcoming route. Based on this design, we propose FS-Nav, a future-state world modeling framework that predicts waypoint-corridor states from spatial memory and language instructions, and communicates them to a VLM navigator through top-down and first-person interfaces. Experiments on standard VLN benchmarks demonstrate that FS-Nav achieves state-of-the-art performance. This highlights navigation-relevant future-state modeling as a promising direction for representing the future in VLN.

Introduction Vision-Language Navigation~(VLN)~ anderson2018vision,ku2020room requires an embodied agent to follow natural-language instructions and navigate to a target location in previously unseen 3D environments. Advances in vision-language models~(VLMs) have driven remarkable progress in VLN through their strong multimodal understanding and reasoning capabilities. Recent methods~ wei2025streamvln,zhang2024navid,wu2026dual therefore adopt VLMs as navigation backbones, directly mapping visual observations and language instructions to navigation actions. Despite these advances, directly predicting actions from current observations remains largely reactive~ li2025regnav,lin2026bat , without explicitly anticipating what may lie ahead. Navigation world models address this limitation by predicting possible future outcomes before action selection. Early approaches synthesize future egocentric views at the pixel level, providing explicit look-ahead signals for navigation~ bar2025navigation,liu2025navforeseeunifiedvisionlanguageworld . Such fine-grained generation requires predicting every visual detail, which is difficult to anticipate and may be unnecessary for downstream decisions. More recent methods~ yao2025navmorph,assran2025vjepa2selfsupervisedvideo move beyond pixel reconstruction by predicting future visual representations in latent space. By abstracting away low-level appearance variations, they focus prediction on more stable, high-level visual content. These advances make world models a powerful foundation for embodied intelligence. Despite this progression, both pixel- and latent-level approaches define the future through observations. We wonder whether predicting what the agent will see is the ultimate form to represent the future in VLN. A principled answer is suggested by predictive cognitive maps. Brown et al. found that the human hippocampus prospectively represents both future goals and intervening locations along the planned route during goal-directed navigation~ brown2016prospective . Predictive-map theory further describes a spatial state through the future states expected to be occupied under a behavior policy~ stachenfeld2016hippocampus . Together, these findings suggest that navigation can organize the future around goal-directed spatial states and route structure, rather than only future views. Inspired by this perspective, we represent the navigation-relevant future at two complementary horizons: a short-horizon waypoint that specifies the next local state to reach, and a mid-horizon corridor that captures the spatial support of the upcoming route. Together, they form a compact, goal-conditioned abstraction of future navigation states, describing where the agent should move next and how the route should unfold, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:motivation (a). Based on this representation, we propose FS-Nav, a future-state world modeling framework for VLN. FS-Nav consists of three components: a Future State World Model predicts waypoint-corridor states from the agent's accumulated spatial memory and language instruction; a Future State Renderer converts the predicted future state into two visual interfaces: a top-down canvas for explicit spatial planning and a first-person visual overlay for egocentric grounding. Finally, a Future-State-Guided Navigator consumes the resulting guidance together with visual observations and the instruction to predict navigation actions. This design separates what the world model predicts from how the prediction is visually grounded for navigation. As previewed in Figure~ fig:motivation (b) and (c), this compact representation is both efficient to predict and effective for navigation. Our contributions are summarized as follows. Drawing inspiration from predictive cognitive maps, we introduce a cognitively grounded perspective on navigation world modeling that organizes the anticipated future around goal-directed spatial states and route structure. We propose FS-Nav, which instantiates this perspective with a short-horizon waypoint and a mid-horizon corridor, predicts them from spatial memory and language instructions, and renders them through top-down and first-person interfaces to guide a VLM navigator. Extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE demonstrate that FS-Nav achieves state-of-the-art performance, validating the effectiveness of navigation-relevant future-state modeling for VLN. Related Works Vision-Language Navigation. Vision-Language Navigation~(VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow natural-language instructions in unseen environments~ anderson2018vision,lyu2026instruction . Earlier methods rely on modular perception and planning pipelines~ li2026think or select actions from predefined navigable candidates~ an2024etpnav . Recent advances in vision-language models~(VLMs) have enabled more unified navigation agents that directly map language instructions and visual histories to actions~ wei2025streamvln,wei2025ground,li2026spaact . These methods improve embodied decision making through stronger temporal modeling, instruction grounding, and action prediction. However, they primarily reason from observations collected so far to determine what to do next, making navigation largely reactive. The spatial structure of the upcoming route is not explicitly modeled before action generation, but remains implicit within the VLM's reasoning process. In contrast, FS-Nav explicitly predicts the upcoming navigation space as a waypoint--corridor future state, providing the VLM navigator with predictive route guidance before action generation. Waypoint- and Route-Guided VLN. Continuous VLN methods commonly introduce intermediate spatial outputs to bridge instruction following and low-level control. Learned waypoint methods predict local navigable candidates or motion targets that are selected by a navigation policy and executed through a controller~ krantz2021waypoint,hong2022bridging,an2024etpnav,lyu2026himemvln . Recent approaches extend this formulation through image-grounded goals, short trajectories, or global route prediction. Goal2Pixel~ bao2026goal2pixel predicts a visible goal pixel that is back-projected into a waypoint and tracked by a local planner, while NavOne~ zhan2026navone predicts global path and goal distributions from top-down maps. FS-Nav also predicts waypoint--corridor geometry, but assigns it a different role. Rather than treating the prediction as the navigation decision or a directly executable plan, FS-Nav represents it as a multi-horizon future state that provides predictive context to a closed-loop VLM navigator. This design makes the upcoming route explicit while preserving the VLM's ability to adapt its actions to the instruction, real observations, and navigation history. World Models in VLN. World models enable navigation agents to anticipate possible outcomes before acting. Pixel-level world models explicitly synthesize future views. PathDreamer~ koh2021pathdreamer generates observations at unvisited viewpoints, while Navigation World Models~(NWM)~ bar2025navigation predict action-conditioned egocentric videos. Although intuitive, pixel-level generation requires reconstructing high-dimensional appearance details that may be redundant or irrelevant to navigation. Latent-level world models reduce this burden by predicting future visual features or latent dynamics rather than raw RGB observations~ yao2025navmorph,zhang2025latent,zhang2026rae,hao2026latentpilot . title: GenPA: Image Generators as Efficient Robot Policies
summary: Pretrained visual generation models have shown great promise in robotic manipulation. However, a representative line of work still treats future visual prediction as the central link between visual generative pretraining and action learning, retaining it as a training objective even when future scenes are no longer generated at inference time. We argue that the instruction-following, spatial understanding, and visual imagination capabilities acquired through image generation pretraining can support control without future visual prediction: image generation models themselves can be directly adapted into powerful action learners. Building on this perspective, we propose GenPA, which fine-tunes an image generation backbone with a lightweight 19M-parameter action regression adapter and reuses its native generative objective for perception co-training. The native image-editing interface accommodates different visual targets without task-specific perception heads, enabling comparisons of current-scene perception, future prediction, and their combinations within a common policy architecture. At deployment, GenPA requires only a single backbone forward pass and action regression, without visual generation or iterative action denoising. Without additional large-scale robot-data pretraining, GenPA demonstrates strong control performance and robustness to perturbations across simulation benchmarks (99.10% success on LIBERO and 83.79% on LIBERO-Plus) and real-world manipulation tasks. Under compiled inference, GenPA takes 20.9 ms per action chunk on a single H100 GPU, achieving 1.7-3.4x speedups over strong VLA and WAM baselines. Our latency analysis further highlights architectural advantages of visual generation backbones for efficient robot control. Ablations across visual tasks and their combinations identify current-depth supervision as a simple, effective training recipe.

Beyond synthesizing realistic images, these models can identify objects referred to in language, follow spatial constraints, and visualize instructed changes to a scene~ xiao2025omnigen,blackforestlabs2025fluxkontext,zhao2026qwenimage2 . As illustrated in Figure~ fig:genpa-overview (a), given a robot manipulation instruction and a corresponding editing request, an image generation system can depict the scene after task completion or sketch end-effector motion paths on the current image. These behaviors suggest that the spatial understanding and visual imagination capabilities acquired through generative pretraining may provide valuable priors for robot action learning. Pretrained image and video generation models have both been adapted for robot control. A representative line of work treats future visual prediction as the central link between generative pretraining and action learning, using generated visual subgoals to guide goal-conditioned policies~ black2023susie or decoding actions from predicted visual transitions through inverse dynamics~ li2026lingbotva . Several methods jointly predict future observations and actions within a shared generative model~ shen2025videovla,kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026dreamzero . Recent approaches further reduce or bypass future visual generation at deployment while retaining future prediction as a co-training objective~ yuan2026fastwam,zhang2026imagewam,ye2026gigaworldpolicy . title: NavRSI: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have enabled vision-and-language navigation (VLN) through direct closed-loop perception and action. However, navigation performance depends strongly on the harness governing LLM-environment interactions, while existing harnesses largely rely on manually designed navigation tools, memory, and agent roles. We introduce NavRSI, a harness-centric recursive self-improvement framework that optimizes the navigation behavior of frozen LLMs through closed-loop experience. In each round, NavRSI iteratively collects navigation trajectories and failure diagnostics, employs a designer agent to rewrite the harness, and retains the revisions that prove effective, while the designer accumulates experience from previous revisions so that the harness and this experience co-evolve. Privileged simulator diagnostics guide only the designer and remain inaccessible to the navigating LLM, enabling deployment with a single RGB camera and primitive actions, without task-specific model training or additional navigation tools. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across LLMs from four vendors, with 85.64% success rate on the full R2R-CE val-unseen split with GPT-6-Astra, surpassing the previously reported best by 4.13%. Evaluations on RxR-CE, NavRAG-CE, and a real humanoid robot further demonstrate its generalizability.

Existing approaches either train specialized navigation models on large-scale embodied data~ hong2022bridging,an2025etpnav,zhang2024navid,cheng2025navila,wei2026streamvln,zhang2025embodied,qwennav or construct explicit navigation workflows around general-purpose large language models (LLMs)~ zhou2024navgpt,chen2024mapgpt,long2024instructnav,qiao2025opennav,shi2025smartway . Frontier LLMs such as GPT-6-Astra and Fable-5.2 have recently opened up a promising alternative, where the LLM directly perceives visual observations and executes primitive actions through closed-loop interaction~ zhou2026embodied . This is enabled by a harness (such as Codex CLI and Claude Agent SDK), i.e., the program that connects the LLM to the environment and decides its context, tools, and feedback~ zhong2026ai,zhou2026navgpt3 . The design of this harness thus becomes an important factor in translating the capabilities of LLMs into successful navigation~ li2026agenticnav,chen2026harnessvln,zhao2026navharness,shi2026navharness . However, existing harness-based VLN methods~ zhou2026embodied,li2026agenticnav,chen2026harnessvln,zhao2026navharness,shi2026navharness,zhou2026navgpt3,sheng2026ask largely rely on human-designed assumptions about what an LLM needs to navigate successfully. They introduce auxiliary tools for depth estimation, waypoint execution, or learned navigation policies~ li2026agenticnav,chen2026harnessvln,zhou2026navgpt3,cheng2026asena , maintain explicit spatial or episodic memories~ chen2026harnessvln,zhao2026navharness,sheng2026ask , or divide navigation into specialized agent roles~ shi2026navharness,chen2026harnessvln,zhou2026navgpt3 . Although effective, these designs prescribe how the LLM should perceive, remember, and act, rather than identifying its limitations from actual interaction with the environment. Importantly, the same LLM performs very differently under different harnesses. As shown in (a), GPT-5.6-Sol achieves success rates of 56.7 and 58.7 with Codex CLI and Mini-swe-agent, but reaches 68.0 with our NavRSI harness on the same primitive actions. The harness itself can thus be a significant bottleneck, raising a fundamental question: Answering this question is challenging because navigation failures emerge from long-horizon interactions between perception, reasoning, and action. An agent may repeatedly attempt blocked movements, lose track of its heading, revisit explored locations, or stop before reaching the destination. Such failures are difficult to anticipate through static prompt design, and an overall success score gives limited guidance on how the harness should be revised. Moreover, the simulator diagnostics that explain these failures are unavailable to the deployed robot, so the optimization must produce a harness that operates without privileged information. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has recently shown promise for optimizing agent code and execution scaffolds~ zelikman2023self,zhang2025darwin,lee2026meta , yet applying it to embodied navigation must account for the sequential, partially observable, and physically grounded nature of this interaction. In this paper, we introduce NavRSI, that keeps the LLM frozen and iteratively rewrites the executable harness around it from closed-loop navigation experience, instead of modifying the model or adding navigation tools. As shown in , NavRSI starts from a general-purpose Mini-swe-agent harness~ zhou2026embodied and alternates between three steps: (1) running navigation episodes to collect closed-loop trajectories and failure diagnostics, (2) employing a designer agent to analyze them and generate revised harness candidates, and (3) evaluating the candidates to retain effective improvements. The designer also maintains a record of its optimization experience, including observed failure patterns, the hypotheses behind its revisions, and evidence of their effectiveness, so that the harness and this experience co-evolve across rounds. To bridge the gap between optimization and deployment, the designer, a separate LLM, reads execution logs and simulator diagnostics (e.g., distance to the goal) from training episodes, whereas the frozen LLM, as the navigator, never sees these privileged signals and relies solely on RGB observations and action feedback. Through this process, NavRSI discovers a lightweight harness that provides action feedback, progress tracking, and arrival verification, without requiring task-specific model training, additional navigation tools, or specialized agent roles. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of NavRSI. Evaluations on , ~ wang2025navrag , and a Unitree G1 humanoid robot further demonstrate cross-dataset and sim-to-real transfer. Ablations show that its components are complementary and that closed-loop RSI outperforms one-shot writing. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We investigate the harness as an optimization target and introduce NavRSI, which improves the runtime interaction of frozen LLMs from their closed-loop navigation behavior, without task-specific model training. We develop an iterative optimization framework in which a designer agent analyzes navigation failures, rewrites executable harness code, and accumulates experience from previous revisions. Simulator diagnostics guide only the designer and are never visible to the navigator, which bridges optimization and deployment. NavRSI discovers a lightweight harness that operates with a single RGB camera and primitive actions, achieving strong performance across multiple LLM families, VLN benchmarks, and real-world environments, with competitive runtime efficiency. VLN was first studied on discrete navigation graphs~ anderson2018vision and later extended to continuous environments with low-level actions~ krantz2020beyond,anderson2020rxr . Trained methods have progressed from waypoint-based models with panoramic RGB-D inputs~ hong2022bridging,an2025etpnav to video-based models with a monocular camera~ zhang2024navid,zhang2025uninavid,cheng2025navila,wei2026streamvln and navigation foundation models trained on millions of samples~ zhang2025embodied,omninav,qwennav . Both lines fit the model to the task, whereas NavRSI trains no model and lets a frontier LLM navigate with one RGB camera and primitive actions. -based navigation. As frontier LLMs learn to act in closed loop through tool calls, the design effort moves from the workflow to the harness~ zhong2026ai . MIP~ zhou2026embodied gives the LLM a minimal interface for observing and stepping, and runs it in harnesses ported from coding agents, such as Codex CLI and Mini-swe-agent. title: ReActWAM: Action-Consistent Caching for Efficient World-Action Models
summary: World-action models (WAMs) often generate future visual states alongside robot actions, introducing substantial computational overhead during inference. During closed-loop execution, consecutive inference cycles often predict similar action sequences, leading to redundant computation. However, reducing this redundancy requires distinguishing consistent actions from changes that demand fresh computation. To address these challenges, we propose ReActWAM, a training-free framework that combines action-intent-guided prefix skipping with inner-chunk prediction reuse. A coarse-to-fine assessment evaluates motion changes, visual consistency, and action prediction conflicts. For eligible chunks, we draw on first-step differences to adapt the cached latent and network features to the current condition, providing an estimate at a later denoising step that bypasses the redundant prefix. Subsequent inference refines this estimate while reusing stable denoising predictions within the chunk. Experiments across LingBot-VA, FastWAM and the Cosmos family on LIBERO-Long and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate $1.41\times$--$5.44\times$ GPU inference speedup, with minimal degradation in task success rates. Real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot further achieve $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup while maintaining success rate.
