Introduction sec:introduction World-action models (WAMs) couple action prediction with future-state modeling to support robotic manipulation~ lyu2025dywa,ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot,li2026lingbotva . However, WAMs commonly rely on iterative generation with denoising-diffusion models~ zhu2025uwm,kim2026cosmospolicy or flow-matching models~ li2026lingbotva,yuan2026fastwam , often involving both actions and future visual states. Repeated forward passes through the denoising network incur substantial latency during closed-loop control, motivating acceleration that preserves task performance. Existing efforts address this cost by training more efficient architectures for future modeling and action prediction~ yuan2026fastwam,ma2026fasterwam,wu2026turbowam , or compressing multi-step generation through distillation and learned calibration~ lyu2026dido,su2026onestepwam . In contrast, training-free methods exploit redundant computation in a frozen model~ ma2024deepcache,zhao2025pab . Diffusion caching identifies similar intermediate features or predictions across denoising steps and reuses them to bypass repeated network computation~ liu2025teacache,lyu2025fastercache,bu2026dicache . However, cached features may not track the evolving denoising state, and their reuse can amplify deviations in action prediction~ ji2026bac,lyu2026dido . Transferring these methods to robot policies therefore requires assessing whether reuse accurately preserves the intended actions. For WAM policies, consecutive inference cycles process chunks comprising action sequences~ yuan2026fastwam and future visual states~ li2026lingbotva,kim2026cosmospolicy . Existing WAM acceleration methods exploit redundancy within and across these chunks to reduce denoising network computation. Within a chunk, prediction caching exploits similar denoising updates at neighboring steps~ ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot . Across chunks, existing methods directly reuse corresponding-step residuals~ zhao2026c3ache , or remap preceding trajectories and select retained states through observation-consistency checks~ liu2026wamachine . These approaches have advanced WAM inference acceleration by exploiting denoising redundancy. Yet visual consistency between current and reference observations does not guarantee action consistency for upcoming behavior, which may require different motion or gripper commands. Reusing the reference information without detecting this change can propagate outdated behavior into subsequent execution. Figure~ fig:outdated_behavior illustrates this mismatch: carrying an open-gripper behavior into a chunk that requires closing can push the object rather than grasp it, despite little change in the scene. This motivates identifying cross-chunk redundancy through action intent, the upcoming behavior predicted from the latest input, especially without reliable overlapping predictions. Effective reuse further requires adapting cached computation to the current input, since compatible intent does not imply identical denoising results. Our central question is: how can action consistency guide redundancy identification, and how should cached computation be corrected for cross-chunk reuse while preserving action quality? To address this question, we propose , a training-free framework for action-consistent caching. A coarse-to-fine gate identifies reusable computation by assessing recent motion and visual consistency, then checking predicted action intent against a cached reference chunk. For accepted chunks, differences between current and reference first-step predictions guide correction of cached states to the current input, providing a later denoising entry that bypasses the redundant prefix. Subsequent inference refines this estimate while reusing stable predictions at neighboring steps. This within-chunk reuse addresses denoising redundancy independently of cross-chunk acceptance. Our contributions are threefold: We identify action consistency, including predicted upcoming behavior, as a criterion for exploiting cross-chunk denoising redundancy. We develop , a training-free framework that combines prediction-guided correction with complementary reuse across and within chunks. Experiments on three WAM families across LIBERO and RoboTwin demonstrate -- GPU inference speedup with comparable task success, alongside end-to-end speedup on the Franka Research 3 robot. title: TrajRealm: A Large-Scale Point Tracking Dataset with Diverse Dynamics
summary: General-purpose point tracking requires large-scale training data with diverse dynamics, yet existing datasets struggle to combine rich dynamic content, accurate scene geometry, and sufficient scale. We introduce TrajRealm, the first public synthetic point-tracking dataset to reach the ten-million-frame scale, constructed from games and embodied simulations. TrajRealm uses the rich environments and motion systems of modern games to capture diverse targets, activities, and interactions across diverse worlds, while embodied simulations add robot manipulation and indoor navigation data. The dataset provides RGB observations, depth, camera parameters, and persistent 2D and 3D point trajectories. These annotations provide precise, geometrically consistent supervision across foreground objects and static environmental surfaces. We also build TrajRealm-Bench with eight subcategories under Interaction and Locomotion to evaluate tracking across diverse scenes. Benchmark evaluations reveal the strengths and limitations of existing trackers in handling complex motion and maintaining long-term point correspondences. Training on TrajRealm improves the performance of existing tracking methods on synthetic and real-world benchmarks.

Training on TrajRealm improves the performance of existing tracking methods on synthetic and real-world benchmarks. Highlights of TrajRealm. TrajRealm covers complex motion, diverse targets and worlds, and multiple viewpoints, with point trajectories on foreground objects and environmental surfaces. fig:trajrealm-showcase Introduction sec:introduction Point tracking follows the same physical points across video frames, providing correspondences for understanding object motion, scene dynamics, and 3D structure~ harley2022pips,doersch2022tapvid . Despite recent advances in general-purpose trackers~ karaev2025cotracker3,zhang2025tapip3d , interactions, deformation, occlusion, and camera motion still make accurate tracking difficult. Further progress requires large-scale training data covering diverse motions, interactions, and environments. To address this need, early work explored manual annotation of point trajectories in real-world videos~ doersch2022tapvid . Although these videos capture diverse dynamics and scenes, annotating trajectories and obtaining depth and camera poses for 3D supervision are costly, making such datasets difficult to scale~ koppula2024tapvid3d . Building dynamic scenes in rendering engines enables large-scale data generation with ground-truth 3D point trajectories~ zhao2026synthverse,jiang2026syn4d,greff2022kubric,zheng2023pointodyssey,jiang2026omnix . However, reproducing diverse real-world scenes and motions remains difficult. The resulting data may contain unnatural motion, assets with limited detail, and outdoor backgrounds represented by simple textured surfaces rather than full 3D geometry~ zhao2026synthverse,greff2022kubric,zheng2023pointodyssey . Our key observation is that modern games can offer more detailed 3D assets, advanced rendering, and richer motions and interactions than typical simulator scenes, making them a promising source of point-tracking data~ richter2016playing,zhou2025omniworld . Many feature connected worlds with detailed environments, realistic lighting, shadows, and changing weather. Each game offers multiple dynamic scenes, while different games broaden the range of targets, motions, and environments. However, robot manipulation and indoor navigation are less common in games, making embodied simulation data another valuable source for a comprehensive point-tracking dataset~ chen2025robotwin,sun2026omninavbench . Based on these observations, we introduce TrajRealm, a ten-million-frame point-tracking dataset built from game and embodied simulation data. It pairs RGB observations with depth maps, camera parameters, and persistent 2D and 3D point trajectories. As shown in Fig.~ fig:trajrealm-showcase , TrajRealm covers complex motion, diverse targets and virtual worlds, and different viewpoints. Its geometrically consistent trajectories align with RGB observations and cover foreground objects and environmental surfaces. It includes single-view and multiview sequences and provides local SE(3) annotations~ cheng2026mose3 . To evaluate trackers across different dynamic scenes, we build the TrajRealm-Bench with 104,306 frames. We organize its scenes into Interaction and Locomotion based on their main motion patterns. Interaction focuses on relative motion among subjects, objects, and their parts. Contact, joint motion, and occlusion make it difficult to track the same physical points over time. Locomotion focuses on subjects or observers moving through environments and the resulting changes in visible surroundings. Each category has four subcategories based on tracking challenges, targets, and scene settings. Comparisons across these subcategories reveal differences that overall averages can hide. Benchmark evaluations reveal complementary strengths among trackers. Trackers perform best on Embodied, while Hard and Long-horizon yield the lowest APD scores. CoTracker3~ karaev2025cotracker3 outperforms TAPIP3D~ zhang2025tapip3d on Hard and Long-horizon, while TAPIP3D achieves higher 3D accuracy on Group and Plant, highlighting the importance of 3D geometric information. Fine-tuning TAPIP3D on TrajRealm also improves performance on synthetic and real-world benchmarks, with camera-space AJ gains of up to 7.83 percentage points relative to its published baseline. TrackEverything also improves all the average metrics on three real-world minival subsets, demonstrating the value of TrajRealm for training different tracking methods. Our contributions are summarized as follows: A large-scale dataset with diverse dynamics. TrajRealm combines game and embodied simulation data at the ten-million-frame scale, covering diverse motions and interactions with depth and point trajectories for both foreground objects and environmental surfaces. A diverse tracking benchmark. We establish a benchmark with eight subcategories under Interaction and Locomotion to evaluate tracking across different motions, targets, and environments. Systematic experiments and analysis. We analyze the strengths and limitations of existing trackers and show that training on TrajRealm improves performance on synthetic and real-world benchmarks. Related Work sec:related Point Tracking Methods sec:related-methods Learning-based point tracking estimates persistent correspondences through occlusion and complex motion. PIPS~ harley2022pips and TAPIR~ doersch2023tapir estimate trajectories for queried points, while CoTracker3 combines joint tracking with training on pseudo-labeled real videos~ karaev2025cotracker3 . Geometry extends this task beyond image coordinates: DELTA~ ngo2025delta estimates image positions and depth, SpatialTrackerV2~ xiao2025spatialtrackerv2 models camera motion for 3D tracking, and TAPIP3D~ zhang2025tapip3d constructs correspondence features in persistent 3D space. Recent work connects tracking with scene geometry and motion structure. D4RT uses a shared video representation and independent queries to recover 3D positions across time and camera coordinate systems~ zhang2026d4rt . OmniX separates motion from static geometry and predicts dense trajectory fields across views and time from compact dynamic tokens~ jiang2026omnix . MoSE3 jointly learns 3D tracks and rigidity embeddings, then differentiably fits world-space rigid transformations within soft rigid clusters~ cheng2026mose3 . Long videos and flexible observation sets introduce further challenges. TrackEverything maintains persistent world-space scene tracks and merges redundant tracks across temporal windows for dense tracking over long videos~ jain2026trackeverything . ARROW uses order-invariant queries to jointly reconstruct and track points from observations captured at different viewpoints and times~ fradlin2026arrow . Point-Tracking Datasets sec:related-datasets Table~ tab:dataset_comparison summarizes representative point-tracking datasets and benchmarks. TAP-Vid~ doersch2022tapvid and TAPVid-3D~ koppula2024tapvid3d provide real-world benchmarks for 2D and 3D tracking, respectively. AnthroTAP~ kim2026anthrotap expands real-video training supervision by fitting parametric human models and filtering the resulting pseudo-labeled trajectories. Synthetic datasets provide direct access to scene state: Kubric~ greff2022kubric supports controlled scene generation, while PointOdyssey~ zheng2023pointodyssey emphasizes long trajectories with naturalistic motion. Recent datasets broaden scene and motion coverage. SynthVerse~ zhao2026synthverse combines animated-film, embodied manipulation, navigation, and articulated objects. It is currently the largest available synthetic tracking dataset, but most of its data lacks full background geometry. MV-TAP~ koo2026mvtap introduces synthetic training data and real evaluation sets for cross-view tracking, while Art-Kubric~ cheng2026mose3 adds articulated interactions with part-level motion and rigidity labels. OmniX~ jiang2026omnix and Syn4D~ jiang2026syn4d use Unreal Engine to combine animated assets with 3D environments, providing background depth and trajectories for static scene points. OmniX releases its data engine and example assets, but its full training and evaluation datasets and complete scene asset collection remain unreleased. Syn4D releases 1.4M frames across 30 3D environments. TrajRealm draws on realistic game worlds with integrated environments and activities, supplemented by embodied simulations. It provides tracking data at the ten-million-frame scale, with more diverse scenes and motions and consistent geometry across foreground objects and static environmental surfaces. Data Collection and Analysis Figure~ fig:trajrealm-overview presents an overview of TrajRealm. The dataset combines two complementary sources, game sequences (TrajRealm-Game) and embodied simulations (TrajRealm-Embodied), in a unified representation of visual observations, persistent point trajectories, and geometric annotations. Data Source and Collection Game Tracking Data. We collect sequences directly from running games through manual play or automated control. For games with simple controls, we use built-in game AI or external navigation scripts. ReShade-based plugins capture rendering outputs, and plugins tailored to each game engine collect point trajectories without extracting the games' original 3D asset files. For selected games with unstable visual quality, we also use Qwen3.5-Flash to help screen the captured sequences. Embodied Simulation Data. The embodied component draws on selected public datasets for robotic manipulation and indoor navigation. We re-render sequences from these datasets and convert the outputs into the same data representation as the game sequences. These statistics describe only the selected and re-rendered subsets included in TrajRealm, rather than the full source datasets. For multiview data, synchronized frames count each scene state once, while camera frames count observations from all recorded views. To prioritize task coverage while limiting redundancy, we include all available task types in each dataset but re-render at most 20 sequences per task across its perturbation variants. For datasets assembled from multiple sources, each source subset is screened separately. For example, we exclude the lower-quality Matterport-derived subset of OmniNavBench~ sun2026omninavbench and retain its GRScenes data. title: Where Delay Compensation Belongs in a Decentralized Mean-Field-Game Swarm with a Control-Barrier Safety Filter
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the 8th International Workshop on Multi-Agent Path Finding (WoMAPF) at AAAI-27 (non-archival workshop)
summary: Large robot teams are often run as a plan-then-execute stack. We study a decentralized instance for drone swarms, a mean-field-game (MFG) routing field with a per-agent control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filter, when communication is limited by a shared TDMA channel. Neighbors are known only through noisy range and bearing measurements exchanged in round-robin slots, so the frame, and with it the age of every estimate, grows with swarm size. In simulation this delay reaches both layers but breaks only the safety layer. Without delay, swarms of up to 100 agents do not collide, even with each measurement's noise held for a whole frame; with it, stale estimates at the CBF cause collisions beyond a frame period of 125 to 175 ms, or 75 to 100 ms at 100 agents with held noise, and swarm size sets where that limit lies and how steeply collisions rise. At the MFG, staleness makes the local density noisier without biasing it, and throughput drops by at most a tenth. We then compensate with lightweight on-board predictors, from constant-velocity fits to a small learned network, that estimate each neighbor's position from its last broadcasts. A layer-split experiment shows where prediction is needed: at the CBF it restores safety and extends the tolerated frame period by 1.4 to 1.7 times with an untrained constant-velocity fit and about 2.3 with the learned network when the noise is redrawn each step; with noise held for a frame the two extend it about equally, while at the MFG it only refines the congestion correction. A constant wider safety margin, the simplest alternative, makes collisions more frequent in a bottleneck. With the routing solved offline, that layer is robust to the delay because it sees neighbors only through a crowd average; compensation belongs in the safety filter, switched on only above the uncompensated limit, since below it the predictor's own error adds collisions.
full_text: Large robot teams are often run as a plan-then-execute stack: a routing layer tells each agent where to go, and a safety layer keeps agents apart. We study a decentralized instance for drone swarms, a mean-field-game (MFG) routing field with a per-agent control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filter, when communication is limited by a shared TDMA channel. Agents know their neighbors only through noisy range and bearing measurements exchanged in round-robin slots, so the frame, and with it the age of every neighbor estimate, grows with the swarm size. We show in simulation that this delay reaches both layers but breaks only the safety layer. Agents range each other over one shared channel. We then compensate the delay with on-board neighbor predictors. title: Beyond Linear Decodability: Understanding and Improving Instruction Following in World Action Models
summary: World action models (WAMs) exhibit strong manipulation capabilities yet often fail to follow test-time language instructions. Prior work shows that non-following (NF) WAMs encode information about the instructed target, but this information does not control their behavior. By comparing NF WAM with its instruction-following (IF) counterpart, we find that target information is substantially more linearly decodable in IF WAMs, despite being encoded in both. Motivated by this observation, we introduce linear decodability supervision (LDS), a simple yet effective auxiliary training objective that promotes the linear decodability of the instructed target information. On LIBERO-CF, InternW0-$Δ$ with LDS achieves a success rate of 74.6% and a grounding rate of 89.2%, surpassing the strongest baseline by 26.8 and 42.9 percentage points, respectively. The effectiveness of LDS challenges the prevailing interpretation that encoded target information does not contribute to WAMs' behavior. To reconcile this apparent contradiction, we propose a prior-instruction competition mechanism, which explains NF and IF behavior as arising from the dominance of prior and instruction signals, respectively. We provide causal evidence for this mechanism by evaluating two training-free interventions derived from it. We reinterpret LDS through this mechanism, showing that it acts as a form of instruction signal enhancement. Finally, more comprehensive evaluations across diverse manipulation tasks and visual domains demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of LDS.

Introduction sec:intro Instruction following is a fundamental capability of vision-language-action (VLA) models and world action models (WAM), requiring them to manipulate objects according to natural language instructions. Despite their ability to perform complex manipulation tasks~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2601-21998, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2603-16666, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2609-07398 , recent works find that these models have a strong bias to execute training-time instruction, ignoring instructions given at test time~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2602-17659, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2603-00592, DBLP:journals/ral/GlossopCBSL26 . Prior studies on VLAs~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2602-17659, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2606-23641 address this issue by recalibrating attention toward instruction-relevant tokens. However, the mechanisms underlying similar failures in WAMs remain unclear. In the WAM architecture we study, the ones employing Wan~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2503-20314 as their backbone, language is injected into visual representations through cross-attention, rather than competing with visual tokens for attention mass within a shared self-attention operation. To study IF in WAMs, we start from training an IF WAM with collected counterfactual data and comparing its internal states with its non-following (NF) counterparts. Similar to~ jiang2026encodedcontrolrevealinggrounding , we probe instruction-related information across different layers and internal components in WAMs and find both IF and NF WAMs encode such information. However, as shown in Figure~ fig:main , the IF WAM exhibit significantly stronger linear decodability of the instructed-target information than its NF counterpart. Motivated by such observation, we propose Linear-Decodability Supervision (LDS) that directly improves the linear decodability of the intructed-target information as an auxiliary loss along side the flow-matching loss. InternW0- with LDS achieves a success rate of 74.6 and a grounding rate of 89.2 , surpassing the strongest baseline by 26.8 and 42.9 percentage points, respectively. Despite the effectiveness of LDS, these results challenges the prevailing interpretation that encoded target information does not contribute to WAMs' behavior~ jiang2026encodedcontrolrevealinggrounding . We propose a prior–instruction competition mechanism to reconcile such contradiction. Specifically, there are two latent tags, a prior tag and an instruction tag , are attached to the prior-preferred and the instruction-specified visual target, respectively. Here, tags refer to additive components of intermediate visual-token representations. Both of these two tags contribute to WAM's behavior. They compete with each other, and the winning one finally determines the action. Therefore, NF and IF WAMs can be explained as the winning of prior tag and instruction tag , respectively. We validate our proposed hypothesis through two training-free interventions derived from it: (1) enhancing the instruction tag ; (2) transiting the prior tag toward the instructed target. Remarkably, enhancing improves OpenWAM's success/grounding rate from 3.8/7.0 to 53.0/80.0 , while transiting achieves 50.8/84.0 , on a picking-target subset of LIBERO-CF without updating the model's parameters. Together, these results provide causal evidence supporting our proposed mechanism. We further revisit the effectiveness of LDS through this mechanistic lens. Since LDS aims to correctly identify the visual target under counterfactual instructions and the easiest way to do so is to exploit the existing , LDS can be seen as a specific form of enhancing . Finally, we conduct more extensive experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of LDS. On LIBERO-CF, InternW0- equipped with LDS achieves a success/grounding rate of 74.6/89.2 , outperforming the strongest baseline by 26.8 and 42.9 percentage points, respectively. On LangGap and RoboTwin-IF, LDS further demonstrates its effectiveness in both object selection and placement-destination grounding, achieving success rates (SR) of 71.4 and 47.4 with InternW0- , respectively. This implies a more general prior-instruction competition mechanism of visual targets in WAMs. Experiments on RoboTwin-IF and real-world tasks further establish the effectiveness of LDS across diverse visual domains beyond LIBERO-based benchmarks. Evaluations on held-out splits of LIBERO-CF and LangGap demonstrate strong generalization to unseen initial configurations, with LDS maintaining robust performance even in completely out-of-distribution scenes. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: A simple yet effective way to improve IF in WAMs. We propose LDS, an auxiliary training objective that improves IF of WAMs without the need of counterfactual demonstrations collection. Experimental results show LDS outperforming existing methods by a large margin. A novel prior-instruction competing mechanism. We provide a novel way of understanding ``encode but not control'' phenomenon by introducing competition with prior signals. We evaluate the correctness of the proposed mechanism through causal interventions and explain the effectiveness of LDS under such mechanism. Related Works sec:related_work World Action Models. WAMs learn robot policies by jointly modeling visual dynamics and actions, often leveraging pretrained video generation models. DreamZero~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2602-15922 builds on Wan2.1~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2503-20314 , while LingBot-VA~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2601-21998 , Fast-WAM~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2603-16666 , and OpenWAM~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2609-07398 adopt Wan2.2. Their shared architectural foundations motivate our investigation of how instruction information interacts with visual representations to influence action generation. Other WAMs, such as Cosmos Policy~ DBLP:conf/iclr/KimGLLGLLSLFG26 and ImageWAM~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2606-19531 , employ different generative backbones. Our mechanistic findings therefore primarily concern Wan-based WAMs. Instruction Following in Embodied Policies. Recent studies reveal that embodied policies may rely on visual shortcuts rather than faithfully following language instructions. LIBERO-CF~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2602-17659 , LangGap~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2603-00592 , and InstructMove~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2608-22990 expose such failures through instruction-sensitive evaluations, while Counterfactual Action Guidance~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2602-17659 and IGAR~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2603-06001 seek to mitigate them. However, the underlying mechanisms in WAMs remain underexplored. Importantly, decodable information need not causally influence model behavior~ DBLP:journals/tacl/ElazarRJG21 . Recent work~ jiang2026encodedcontrolrevealinggrounding demonstrates this decodability-control gap in both VLAs and WAMs, where instructed targets remain encoded despite visually biased actions. We reveal that LDS leads to substantial IF improvements. title: Mem-X: A Memory-Dependent Cross-Episode Benchmark for Vision-and-Language Navigation
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2027)
summary: Long-term memory enables embodied agents to reuse past observations across tasks. However, existing cross-episode vision-and-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks often leave it unclear whether successful navigation relies on historical memory or current exploration. We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark designed to evaluate memory-dependent cross-episode VLN. Mem-X organizes episodes into sessions in which subsequent instructions refer to objects or routes encountered in earlier episodes. Its three levels evaluate historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization and historical-route reproduction. For the latter two levels, agents receive episode-local poses but no transformations between episode frames, requiring them to establish spatial correspondence with historical memory. Mem-X comprises 2,071 episodes across 710 sessions in 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes. We also provide MemBridge, a modular baseline that combines semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval to support existing VLN agents. Experiments with state-of-the-art VLN methods demonstrate the benefits of MemBridge while revealing substantial room for improvement on memory-dependent navigation. The benchmark and baseline code are available at https://github.com/NJU-R-L-Group-Embodied-Lab/Mem-X.

Introduction Embodied agents that operate in real environments over long horizons need to retain and use observations and experience from past tasks ~ krantz2023ivln,khanna2024goat . When an agent continuously executes tasks in the same scene, different tasks usually share the same locations, and historical memory from preceding episodes can often assist later tasks~ krantz2023ivln . Cross-episode memory is therefore necessary. Traditional VLN benchmarks~ anderson2018r2r,ku2020rxr,jain2019r4r,thomason2020cvdn, qi2020reverie,zhu2021soon usually evaluate each episode independently, and an agent's historical information is used only within the current task, making it difficult to exploit the associations across tasks. Existing cross-episode VLN benchmarks~ krantz2023ivln,hong2025gsa and lifelong navigation benchmarks already allow agents to retain and use historical information. However, these benchmarks usually do not make historical memory necessary for completing later tasks. Relying only on the spatial relations and actions suggested by the current instruction, exploration can achieve the same effect. We therefore consider this task design not tightly coupled with the memory mechanism, and it cannot truly evaluate an algorithm's cross-episode memory ability. To address this issue, we construct Mem-X, a cross-episode VLN benchmark for memory-dependent tasks, as shown in Figure~ fig:overview . Its three levels of increasing difficulty are detailed in Section~ sec:task_design . Unlike existing work, we design Mem-X for tightly coupled memory evaluation. Through memory recall, in-memory and off-memory localization, episode indexing, and historical-path reproduction, it forces the agent to use memory to complete the related tasks. Table~ tab:benchmark_comparison compares Mem-X with existing related benchmarks. To provide a reference baseline for Mem-X, we introduce MemBridge, a modular approach that combines semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval. MemBridge connects historical observations to current navigation tasks and can be integrated with different VLN agents, providing a practical starting point for studying memory-dependent navigation. The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark that makes historical experience an explicit part of VLN task specification through references to previously encountered objects and traversed routes. It comprises 2,071 episodes organized into 710 sessions across 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes. We establish an evaluation protocol that controls access to cross-episode coordinates and assesses both memory-related capabilities and task completion, revealing navigation failures that endpoint-based metrics alone overlook. We provide MemBridge, a modular reference baseline that enables existing VLN agents to use historical memory across episodes. Experiments with four representative agents demonstrate its effectiveness while highlighting substantial room for improvement on Mem-X. Related Work Vision-and-Language Navigation Benchmarks VLN benchmarks typically evaluate each episode independently. R2R~ anderson2018r2r established the classic setting on the discrete Matterport3D~ chang2017matterport3d graph; R4R~ jain2019r4r and RxR~ ku2020rxr extended it to longer and multilingual paths. CVDN~ thomason2020cvdn , REVERIE~ qi2020reverie , and SOON~ zhu2021soon study dialog, remote-object, and goal-oriented variants, while R2R-CE~ krantz2020r2rce and LH-VLN~ song2025lhvln move to continuous and long-horizon settings. In all of these benchmarks, historical information remains limited to a single episode. Cross-Episode Memory and Lifelong Embodied Navigation In addition to independent single-episode settings, existing studies have also begun to explore persistent memory across tasks and lifelong embodied navigation. IVLN~ krantz2023ivln organizes independent episodes from existing VLN datasets into tours that are executed continuously in the same scene, and allows agents to retain and use historical memory across episodes. GSA-R2R~ hong2025gsa evaluates agents that execute a large number of instructions in the same building and perform scene adaptation. LENL~ wang2026lenl is a continual-learning benchmark across scenes and instruction types. GOAT-Bench~ khanna2024goat extends lifelong embodied navigation from the perspective of multimodal sequential-goal navigation. These benchmarks usually treat historical memory only as auxiliary information, and the completion of later tasks does not necessarily depend on historical memory. Some recent work tries to emphasize historical memory. LMEE-Bench~ wang2026lmee accumulates episodic memory along a single multi-goal exploration trajectory and then tests recall with question answering; the memory dependency occurs in QA rather than in later navigation, and it does not constitute a cross-episode setting. FindingDory~ yadav2026findingdory first collects long-horizon interactions, then retrieves a target frame from the historical video and navigates back, which evaluates in-trajectory memory recall quite thoroughly. Its history records include pose, and the agent is also equipped with GPS, so it does not require cross-episode self-localization and memory alignment without a shared global pose. Mem-X instead organizes multiple episodes into sessions with explicit dependencies and adds in-memory / off-memory localization. Memory-Augmented VLN Agents Memory in existing VLN methods is typically implicit temporal memory or explicit spatial memory. Implicit methods encode history inside the model, including recurrent hidden states ~ krantz2020r2rce , Transformer-based history encoding and caching ~ chen2021hamt,lin2021mtvm,zeng2025janusvln , state-space recurrent memory ~ zhang2025cosmo,yao2025navmorph , and multi-timescale memory ~ wei2026streamvln,liu2026memvln,zhang2025uninavid . Explicit methods store memory in external structures, including topological and scene graphs ~ an2024etpnav,chen2022duet,zhou2025fsrvln , metric or semantic maps ~ wang2023gridmm,zhang2025mapnav,wang2024vln3dff , and waypoint-indexed episodic memory ~ ding2026unilavira,xu2025memoir . These mechanisms are mainly used within a single episode, or accumulate maps with pose, and are not designed for memory-dependent tasks across episodes without a shared global pose. Benchmark Task Design sec:task_design Mem-X groups navigation episodes into sessions. Agents accumulate experience during initial tasks and use it in subsequent tasks, whose instructions refer to previously encountered objects or traversed routes. We design three levels that progressively extend historical-object recall to cross-episode localization and historical-route reproduction. All levels provide drift-free poses derived from simulator ground truth. Level 1 uses a shared coordinate frame across episodes to isolate historical-object recall from cross-episode localization. Levels 2 and 3 instead express poses in episode-local frames obtained by resetting the simulator pose. Transformations between episode frames are withheld, requiring agents to establish spatial correspondence with historical observations. Level 1: In-Trajectory Memory Recall. Each session consists of a base episode, Episode 0, followed by 1–4 memory-dependent tasks. These tasks start at the endpoint of the trajectory actually executed in Episode 0 or at a point sampled from its 75 –90 interval. The agent must identify and return to an object referenced through the preceding experience. By placing the start on the historical trajectory and providing a shared coordinate frame, this level focuses on memory construction and target recall while reducing the need for unexplored-region navigation. Level 2: In-Memory Localization and Episodic Indexing. Each session contains three episodes with separate local coordinate frames. Episode 0 provides the initial experience. Episode 1 starts 1.0–1.5 m from the start of the Episode 0 reference trajectory and requires the agent to revisit a target from Episode 0 before following a new navigation instruction. Episode 2 starts at the same position as Episode 1 and refers to a target encountered in Episode 1 but not Episode 0. The agent must relate its current observations to the visited region and retrieve the target associated with the relevant episode. Level 3: Off-Memory Relocalization and Route Re-entry. Each session contains two base episodes whose reference trajectories share a continuous segment, followed by a memory-dependent episode. All three episodes use separate local coordinate frames. Introduction sec:intro Vision--language--action (VLA) models build robot policies on pretrained vision--language models (VLMs), using an action expert to turn the observed scene and the instruction into continuous actions~ black2024pi0 . However, scene--instruction correlations in demonstrations can encourage visual shortcuts, allowing policies to ignore language~ lian2026langforce,zhang2026flatnesspreservesinstructionfollowing . Because the action expert is randomly initialized, it can readily inherit these biases and may, in turn, degrade the pretrained VLM's representations through backpropagation during joint fine-tuning. Action expert pretraining is thus worth exploring to foster language dependence. Existing recipes counter visual shortcuts by controlling which modality the expert sees. APT~ xu2026apt and BayesVLA~ xu2025bayesvla adopt vision--action (VA) pretraining, first learning a visuomotor prior and then introducing language. Conversely, LA4VLA~ lin2026la4vla uses language--action (LA) pretraining without vision to learn instruction--action associations, exploring both sequential and mixed LA--VLA training. Despite their differences, these methods follow the same paradigm of incorporating a unimodal pretraining stage preceding full pretraining. However, single-modality staging can damage the pathway needed to combine vision and language. For an instruction such as ``pick up the cup that is the same color as the plate,'' VA pretraining provides the scene without the instruction specifying color matching, while LA pretraining provides the instruction without the visual evidence needed to identify the matching cup. Neither stage directly supervises this joint computation, yet the parameters supporting it continue to change. The risk is therefore not merely that joint modeling is left untrained, but that its pathway can be shut down. Under the specified population gradient flow, subsequent full-input training cannot reopen it, even with unlimited adaptation. This raises a question: can action expert pretraining mitigate visual shortcuts while preserving joint vision--language modeling? We answer with Stochastic Context for Action Expert Pretraining (SCAP). SCAP follows a two-stage training scheme: we first pretrain the action expert by randomly masking both visual and text tokens, then continue training with full visual and language inputs. By varying the visibility of both modalities, this pretraining exposes the expert to diverse combinations of visual and linguistic cues, discouraging visual shortcuts while retaining joint supervision whenever complementary cues remain visible (Fig.~ fig:scap_motivation ). VA, LA, and full-input pretraining are special cases of SCAP obtained with different mask distributions. In the same construction, SCAP meets both requirements. First, if masks retain both joint cues sufficiently often, the joint modeling path never closes (Sec.~ sec:prevention ). Second, random masking gives cues from either modality a chance of being hidden, reducing overreliance on a single modality. This advantage persists through subsequent full-input adaptation (Sec.~ sec:shortcut ). Experiments demonstrate that SCAP outperforms alternative pretraining methods, with consistent gains across four VLA architectures and multiple model scales. By intervening on test-set instructions, we further show that SCAP improves robustness to paraphrasing and sensitivity to changes in task intent. On three real-robot manipulation tasks, SCAP achieves an average success rate of 76.67 , exceeding full-input pretraining by 25 percentage points. title: BladeR: Scalable, Shape-Guided 3D Reconstruction of Wind Turbine Blades from UAV Imagery
summary: The structural integrity of wind turbine blades is critical for safe, efficient energy production. Accurate 3D reconstruction allows precise localization and quantification of wear and early damage detection. While drone-based inspections are standard, their high-resolution imagery poses challenges such as weak texture, lighting variability, and high computational cost. We present BladeR, a scalable pipeline for high-quality 3D reconstruction from inspection imagery. A hierarchical sparse reconstruction strategy leverages GPS/IMU data and blade shape priors to guide advanced keypoint matchers on full-resolution images. For dense reconstruction, a tiled Gaussian Splatting framework processes 45 MP images at native resolution, isolates the blade from background, and adaptively enhances detail recovery along the leading edge. Validation against commercial and open-source baselines shows significant improvements in model completeness and detail.
full_text: BladeR: Scalable, Shape-Guided 3D Reconstruction of Wind Turbine Blades from UAV Imagery Jonathan Sterckx , Michiel Vlaminck and Hiep Luong IPI-URC-imec, Ghent University, Sint-Pietersnieuwstraat 41, Ghent, Belgium \ jonathan.sterckx, michiel.vlaminck, hiep.luong\ @ugent.be 0 This is the authors' version of the paper published in Proceedings of the 21st International Conference on Computer Vision Theory and Applications (VISAPP 2026) -- Volume~3, pages 119--130. DOI: 10.5220/0014309700004084 . Paper published under CC license (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0). Proceedings Copyright ~2026 by SCITEPRESS -- Science and Technology Publications, Lda. -1 INTRODUCTION Wind energy is a critical component of the global transition to renewable energy gwec2024globalwind . The operational efficiency and lifespan of wind turbines depend heavily on blade integrity. Leading edge erosion, for example, degrades aerodynamic performance, reduces energy output and shortens blade lifespan herring2019increasing , ozccakmak2024determination , making regular inspections essential shafiee2019maintenance . Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have revolutionized turbine inspections by providing safer, faster, and more cost-effective alternatives to manual methods poleo2021estimating . While 2D drone images are useful for detecting surface defects xu2019wind , memari2024review , full 3D reconstructions offer richer insights by enabling precise volumetric quantification, defect localization, and differentiation between true damage and surface artifacts sterckx2025segmentation . They also support defect tracking and blade deformation analysis, enabling more comprehensive digital twin models, with room to advance beyond current 2D techniques hu2025digital . Prior studies demonstrate the feasibility of photogrammetry for blade reconstruction nielsen2020high , zhang2020quantifying , but often rely on decommissioned blades under controlled conditions, without a scalable pipeline. sterckx2025accurate proposed a custom reconstruction pipeline with improved accuracy, yet it does not leverage domain-specific knowledge and its applicability remains limited to small datasets. To address these limitations, we present a pipeline tailored to real-world inspections and validated on a new UAV dataset. Our contributions are: A high-overlap UAV dataset of two operational blades captured with a 45 MP camera under varied conditions. A scalable preprocessing pipeline that uses automated segmentation and blade-centered tiling to enable full-resolution image processing without exceeding memory limits. A robust two-stage sparse reconstruction that leverages GPS data and a blade-geometry prior to concentrate keypoint matching along the leading edge, reducing the number of required image-matching operations. A custom Gaussian Splatting framework with soft background masking, blade-specific adaptive densification, and tiled full-resolution processing, allowing reconstruction at resolutions significantly higher than those supported by standard dense reconstruction methods. Our method produces more complete and detailed 3D models than leading commercial and open-source software, while scaling effectively to high-resolution imagery and large inspection datasets—providing a solid foundation for improved damage assessment and maintenance planning. RELATED WORK Only a few works have addressed image-based 3D reconstruction of wind turbine blades. zhang2020quantifying studied how lighting and image blur affect UAV-based photogrammetric reconstruction. Their experiments used a decommissioned blade section indoors, combining natural and artificial textures. 3D models were generated with Agisoft Metashape metashape and compared against a high-precision 3D-scanned reference. nielsen2020high performed a feasibility study using high-resolution SfM and MVS with Agisoft Metashape to evaluate leading-edge roughness on a decommissioned blade tip with simulated erosion. Their data was collected outdoors with a handheld camera. hung2025three explored a multimodal approach, capturing visible and thermal images of a small rooftop turbine using UAVs. They applied NeRF mildenhall2021nerf to visible imagery and projected thermal views onto the geometry to localize defects. While promising for multimodal inspection, the resulting 3D models lacked the accuracy needed for precise defect measurement. sterckx2025accurate proposed a custom reconstruction pipeline outperforming off-the-shelf tools in accuracy and robustness. They introduced hierarchical keypoint tracking to handle low-texture regions and variable illumination, and a Gaussian Splatting variant with foreground isolation for dense reconstruction. However, their approach was limited to small datasets, relied on computationally intensive matching, required downscaling (losing critical detail) and did not incorporate blade-specific enhancements. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces a high-overlap UAV dataset of an operational blade under realistic conditions and an enhanced pipeline with foreground-aware tiling, blade geometry-informed matching, and blade-specific dense reconstruction improvements, achieving greater scalability and fidelity. PRELIMINARIES 3D reconstruction from multi-view images typically involves two stages: sparse reconstruction using Structure from Motion (SfM), and dense reconstruction via Multi-View Stereo (MVS) or newer alternatives like Gaussian Splatting (GS). Sparse 3D Reconstruction SfM reconstructs a sparse 3D point cloud and camera poses from overlapping images SfM_survey , as illustrated in Fig. fig:high_level_pipeline (middle). An incremental SfM pipeline colmap typically involves: Keypoint detection and description: Image features are extracted using algorithms such as SIFT sift or ORB orb , which encode the appearance of local image regions into high-dimensional descriptors. Keypoint matching: Keypoint descriptors are matched across image pairs, using nearest-neighbor search or neural networks sarlin2020superglue , lindenberger2023lightglue . Geometric verification is applied to discard outlier matches. Incremental reconstruction: Starting from an image pair, their relative pose is estimated and corresponding points are triangulated. Additional images are registered via PnP pnp , extending the cloud. Outliers are rejected via RANSAC ransac . Bundle adjustment: Global optimization refines 3D points and camera poses intrinsics to minimize reprojection error bundle_adjustment . Popular open-source SfM systems include COLMAP colmap , while Agisoft Metashape metashape is a widely used commercial alternative. Recent methods such as Pixel-Perfect SfM pixel_perfect_sfm , Detector-Free SfM detectorfreesfm , MASt3R leroy2024grounding , and VGGT wang2025vggt leverage deep learning for improved accuracy, robustness, and speed, but their reliance on neural networks limits scalability to high-resolution imagery. This work introduces a hybrid approach to overcome these scalability challenges, integrating traditional SfM with deep learning-based matchers using a tile-based strategy. Dense 3D Reconstruction Dense reconstruction generates detailed surfaces from the input images and sparse reconstruction outputs. Traditionally, Multi-View Stereo (MVS) computes dense depth maps by matching pixels across multiple views and then fuses the depth maps into a detailed 3D representation MVS_survey . More recently, Gaussian Splatting (GS) kerbl20233d models the scene with 3D Gaussians initialized on SfM points. These Gaussians are iteratively optimized in location, shape, and opacity so that renderings match input images (illustrated in Fig. fig:high_level_pipeline , right), using a combination of and losses with differentiable rendering. Adaptive Gaussian splitting, cloning, and pruning balances detail and memory usage. By default, GS minimizes photometric error without enforcing geometric constraints, which can cause artifacts in low-coverage regions (“floating” or “needle” Gaussians) mip_splatting . Extensions address these issues: Mip-Splatting mip_splatting applies 3D low-pass filtering; Deblur-GS deblur_gs and BAD-Gaussians bad_gaussians improve robustness to defocus and motion blur; 2DGS 2dgs uses surface-oriented Gaussians with novel regularization. Compared to MVS, GS is faster and provides a flexible framework to handle challenging imaging conditions such as blur and lighting variation. Unlike NeRF nerf , which encodes a 3D scene implicitly in the weights of a neural network and generates novel views by querying the network with a 5D vector (position and viewing direction), GS offers an explicit representation, making the underlying structure directly accessible. This facilitates tasks such as defect localization and surface analysis, making it particularly well-suited for wind turbine blade inspection. METHODS This section describes the data collection process and our 3D reconstruction pipeline, BladeR, covering data preprocessing as well as sparse and dense reconstruction stages. Figure~ fig:high_lvl_diagram provides a high-level overview of BladeR, illustrating the workflow from preprocessing through to dense 3D reconstruction. Data Collection To develop and evaluate a 3D reconstruction pipeline for real-world inspections, we acquired high-overlap UAV images of two operational wind turbine blades using a DJI Zenmuse P1 camera (45 MP, 35 mm focal length) mounted on a drone with integrated GPS and IMU sensors. Accurate 3D reconstruction requires multiple viewpoints, but dense coverage is impractical due to drone battery limits and inspection time. Since wear mainly occurs along the leading edge, we fly multiple lines capturing it from a frontal angle (angle 1 in Fig.~ fig:high_level_pipeline , left), azimuthal angles (2 and 3), and polar oblique angles (4 and 5). Representative images from each flight line are shown in Fig. fig:image_samples . Blade 1 (vertical, cloudy conditions) includes 104 images from two azimuthal and two polar angles, whereas Blade 2 (horizontal, sunny conditions) includes 121 images from two azimuthal and one polar angle. Preprocessing subsection:preprocessing Sparse 3D reconstruction begins with keypoint detection and matching. To improve robustness, we apply two preprocessing steps: background masking and image tiling (Fig.~ fig:preprocessing ). Background masking produces a binary mask ( = background, = foreground) to isolate the blade, mitigate dynamic backgrounds (e.g., clouds, nearby turbines), and constrain keypoint matching to foreground regions, improving correspondence quality. Image tiling divides each image into patches to: (1) reduce computation by avoiding large background areas, and (2) preserve local detail, since deep keypoint detectors are trained on low-resolution inputs ( 1 MP) and downscaling full images would remove fine blade structure. We compute coarse masks using DepthAnythingV2 yang2024depth on downscaled images. Unlike prior work that relies on a static depth threshold to separate foreground from background sterckx2025accurate , we adopt a dynamic seeded region-growing strategy adams1994seeded : starting from the closest pixel (the seed), the mask expands while depth gradients remain below a threshold , improving segmentation when blade and background depths overlap (see Fig. fig:preprocessing ). For foreground-focused tiling, the coarse mask (upscaled) guides extraction of the blade’s principal axis via PCA. Patch centers are sampled along this axis at stride , tiles of size are extracted, and only patches overlapping the foreground are retained (Alg.~ alg:tiling ). Finally, masks are refined using Segment Anything (SAM) kirillov2023segment on native-resolution tiles, using the coarse mask as a prompt to produce sharper fine masks. title: PanoUAV-Track: Full-Spherical UAV Visual Tracking in the Wild
summary: Existing UAV tracking benchmarks predominantly rely on perspective cameras with limited fields of view. Omnidirectional cameras enable full-spherical observation, yet tracking from moving UAV platforms remains largely unexplored. Unlike ground-level panoramic tracking, UAV-mounted omnidirectional cameras observe targets across both azimuth and elevation, introducing geometric challenges under equirectangular projection (ERP). To investigate this setting, we capture approximately \textbf{40 hours of real-world 8K panoramic UAV video} and construct \textbf{PanoUAV-Track} through temporal clip extraction, target annotation, and the integration of simulated sequences. The resulting benchmark comprises 1,895 sequences, 507,961 frames, and 2,872 annotated objects, covering real-world daytime and nighttime scenes alongside simulation, and supporting both visual and language-based target specification. Through extensive evaluations, we reveal a clear \textbf{perspective-to-spherical} generalization gap and identify tracking degradation associated with latitude-dependent distortion and ERP seam discontinuity. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{PanoUAV-Tracker (PUTrack)}, a geometry-aware tracking framework combining latitude-adaptive search and seam-aware periodic sampling. PUTrack improves zero-shot and in-domain tracking, particularly for seam-crossing targets. Code and benchmark resources will be available\footnote{\textcolor{tabpink}{https://libingyu01.github.io/PanoUAV-Track/}}.

Introduction sec:introduction Visual object tracking from unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) has witnessed substantial progress in recent years, driven by advances in tracking algorithms and aerial tracking benchmarks mueller2016benchmark,zhang2022webuav,li2024uavnlt, wu2025ort,xue2025sglatrack,AIFlowAn,AIFlowShao . However, existing benchmarks and tracking methods predominantly rely on perspective cameras with limited fields of view li2024uavnlt,li2025stitchfusion,li2026exploring,zhang2022webuav . Under such observations, targets can easily disappear from the image due to UAV motion or changes in viewing direction, even when they remain within the surrounding environment ( (a)). This limitation raises a fundamental question: can visual trackers developed for perspective observations effectively generalize to omnidirectional UAV tracking? Omnidirectional cameras offer a promising solution by capturing the surrounding environment across a complete spherical field of view. Existing panoramic benchmarks, such as 360VOT~ huang2023_360vot , 360VOTS~ xu2025_360vots , and PanoVOS~ yan2024panovos , have advanced object tracking and segmentation under omnidirectional observations. However, these benchmarks primarily focus on general panoramic scenarios rather than dynamic observations from aerial platforms ( (b)). Unlike ground-level panoramic tracking, UAV-mounted omnidirectional cameras experience continuously changing aerial viewpoints, where targets may appear at arbitrary azimuths and elevations ( (c)). We refer to this challenging setting as full-spherical UAV object tracking. Beyond extending the field of view, full-spherical observation introduces fundamentally different tracking challenges. Omnidirectional videos are typically represented using equirectangular projection (ERP), which maps spherical observations onto a rectangular image plane. However, this representation does not preserve the geometric properties of the sphere. As illustrated in (d, e.1--e.3), target appearance varies with latitude under ERP, while seam-crossing targets may appear on opposite sides of the image. Consequently, a target that moves continuously on the sphere may exhibit substantial appearance deformation or abrupt displacement in the projected image. These effects challenge conventional tracking assumptions and raise concerns about the generalization of perspective-based trackers to full-spherical observations. To systematically investigate these challenges, we introduce PanoUAV-Track, a large-scale benchmark for full-spherical UAV visual tracking. The benchmark comprises 1,895 sequences, 507,961 frames, and 2,872 annotated objects, covering 951 daytime, 606 nighttime, and 338 simulated sequences. It provides diverse aerial viewpoints, target trajectories, and observation conditions, together with visual and language-based target specifications. Based on this benchmark, we investigate three fundamental research questions: (RQ1) How well do perspective trackers generalize to full-spherical UAV observations? (RQ2) Does the generalization gap persist across different observation domains? (RQ3) How does spherical projection geometry affect tracking performance? Our comprehensive evaluations reveal a substantial perspective-to-spherical generalization gap, with tracking performance particularly affected by latitude-dependent distortion and ERP seam discontinuities. Motivated by these findings, we further propose PanoUAV-Tracker (PUTrack), a geometry-aware tracking framework specifically designed for full-spherical UAV observations. PUTrack combines template-guided target localization with geometry-aware search construction. Its Geometry-Aware Search Adapter (GASA) incorporates Latitude-Adaptive Patch Sampling (LAPS) to compensate for latitude-dependent distortion and Seam-Aware Search Cropping (SASC) to preserve spatial continuity across panoramic boundaries. Thus, PUTrack maintains coherent target localization in ERP coordinates. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: Full-spherical UAV tracking. We investigate visual tracking using UAV-mounted omnidirectional cameras, extending aerial tracking to full-spherical observations. PanoUAV-Track benchmark and analysis. PanoUAV-Track supports visual and language-based tracking. Extensive evaluations reveal the limitations of perspective trackers under full-spherical observations. PanoUAV-Tracker (PUTrack). A geometry-aware tracking framework is developed with latitude-adaptive search and periodic seam-aware sampling. Related Work sec:related_work Perspective Tracking Visual object tracking has progressed from Siamese architectures to Transformer- and sequence-based frameworks, supported by large-scale benchmarks such as TrackingNet~ muller2018trackingnet , GOT-10k~ huang2019got , and LaSOT~ fan2019lasot . Recent methods further strengthen target modeling and temporal reasoning chen2021transformer,yan2021learning,cui2022mixformer,ye2022joint, chen2023seqtrack,cai2024hiptrack,liang2025autoregressive . UAV benchmarks extend this setting to aerial observation mueller2016benchmark,zhang2022webuav,li2024uavnlt , while vision--language tracking introduces natural-language target specification wang2021tnl2k,feng2021snlt,zhou2023jointnlt,ma2023decoupletnl, ma2024uvltrack,shao2024querynlt,liu2025mambavlt,li2025dutrack . Despite differences in task formulation and model design, these benchmarks remain predominantly based on perspective imagery. PanoUAV-Track complements them by evaluating both visual and language target specification under full-spherical UAV observation. Omnidirectional and Spherical Tracking Omnidirectional tracking extends visual observation beyond perspective cameras while introducing spherical projection challenges. 360VOT~ huang2023_360vot establishes an omnidirectional single-object tracking benchmark with sphere-aware representations and evaluation. 360VOTS~ xu2025_360vots extends this setting to tracking and segmentation, while PanoVOS~ yan2024panovos explores temporal consistency in panoramic video segmentation. Recent studies further investigate omnidirectional tracking on mobile robotic platforms. JRDB-PanoTrack~ le2024jrdb provides panoptic tracking annotations for robot-centered environments, while OmniTrack~ luo2025omnidirectional introduces QuadTrack for omnidirectional multi-object tracking on quadruped robots. title: Beyond a Single Human Demonstration: Learning from Scored Trajectory Alternatives for End-to-End Driving

summary: Human driving logs record only one trajectory per scene, leaving other feasible driving choices without explicit trajectory targets or quality labels. This limits supervision for end-to-end planners that generate and refine multiple candidate trajectories. Meanwhile, conditioning refinement on a large vision-language model adds substantial online inference cost. We propose DriveSTA, which extends autoregressive proposal generation and proposal-conditioned residual flow refinement with scored trajectory alternatives. For each training scene, we generate alternatives offline through smooth deformations of the recorded trajectory and evaluate their simulated execution against logged traffic. Diverse, high-quality alternatives supervise distinct proposals and define residual targets for quality-guided denoising, while candidates spanning the full score range train a scorer to assess driving quality. A shared joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), adapted through masked video-feature prediction, encodes observed frames once and provides temporal context for both refinement and scoring. On NAVSIM v1 Navtest, DriveSTA ranks first among the compared planners trained on NAVSIM data alone. With expanded training data, DriveSTA-Scale achieves state-of-the-art results among the compared methods on Navtest and closed-loop HUGSIM, while reducing mean planner forward-pass latency by 73% relative to ChainFlow-VLA in matched evaluations.

Recent work has combined autoregressive trajectory generation and diffusion-based modeling in two-stage planners that first propose candidate trajectories and then refine them. ChainFlow-VLA~ wang2026chainflow follows this direction, using an autoregressive generator to produce multiple proposals and a proposal-conditioned residual flow model to refine each trajectory as a whole. The effectiveness of this proposal--refinement framework depends on the supervision available for both stages. Although ChainFlow-VLA generates multiple candidates, each driving log records only one human demonstration. Its winner-take-all objective assigns the closest proposal to that reference, leaving other feasible driving choices without explicit trajectory targets. The demonstration alone also provides limited information about the relative quality of these alternatives. To incorporate scene semantics into refinement, ChainFlow-VLA conditions its residual flow model on an online vision-language model (VLM). This semantic guidance improves performance in ambiguous and long-tail scenarios, but running the VLM adds substantial inference cost. Furthermore, refinement in interactive traffic requires context about how surrounding agents move over time. This calls for temporal representations that complement the scene semantics provided by VLMs. We introduce , which retains ChainFlow-VLA's probabilistic formulation and uses scored alternatives to guide both trajectory generation and residual denoising. title: VeilGS: Solving Darkness as a Veil of 2D Basis Maps over Retinex 3DGS
summary: In a dark capture, the darkness is not uniform. How much light reaches a surface depends on where it lies relative to the few light sources, and the camera compresses what remains with a tone curve. Most low-light 3D reconstruction methods either apply one curve to every pixel of a view, so a dark object beside a lamp and a bright one in an unlit corner receive the same correction, or store the darkness in the 3D representation, where it can absorb scene detail. We present VeilGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting method for low-light novel view synthesis that treats the degradation as a veil drawn over a clear scene. Each Gaussian carries an albedo and a shading latent instead of spherical harmonics, separating surface colour from illumination. Each view is darkened by a spatially varying gain followed by a global tone curve, and rendering without this veil gives the restored scene. A small network predicts a coarse basis for the gain from the observation, and its coefficients are solved for each view rather than learned. Training through this solve discourages the Gaussians from absorbing what the veil can explain. VeilGS needs no paired normal-light supervision and stores no per-view parameters. On Gaussian-DK, its restored renders score best on no-reference NIQE and CLIP-IQA and are rated highest in a blind user study with 55 participants. On LOM, it achieves results competitive with the state of the art.

Introduction sec:intro Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~ Mildenhall2021NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ Kerbl2023 have brought unprecedented progress to novel view synthesis, with applications from virtual reality to autonomous driving and robotics. However, both methods require well-exposed inputs. In settings such as nighttime driving, surveillance and robotic exploration of unlit spaces, the captured images are dark, where standard NeRF and 3DGS pipelines fail to produce usable novel views. 3D representations such as NeRF and 3DGS store the colour of each point as it appears to the camera, which causes the darkness to be baked into the representation itself. The darkness is also spatially non-uniform, since surfaces are located at different positions relative to the light sources. Enhancing each image with a 2D low-light method~ Guo2020ZeroDCE,Ma2022SCI,Cai2023Retinexformer before reconstruction is ineffective~ Cui2024AlethNeRF,Wang2023LLNeRF,Cui2025LuminanceGS,Zhou2025LITAGS , because each image is enhanced on its own, which breaks the multi-view consistency that 3D reconstruction relies on, creating floaters and colour drift. To overcome this challenge, several methods handle the degradation inside the 3D representation. LLNeRF~ Wang2023LLNeRF decomposes each 3D point into view-independent and view-dependent components and Aleth-NeRF~ Cui2024AlethNeRF explains darkness with concealing fields, but both inherit the slow training and rendering of NeRF. On 3DGS, Gaussian-DK~ Ye2024GaussianDK decodes a lightness map from per-Gaussian light features and the exposure metadata of each image, Luminance-GS~ Cui2025LuminanceGS learns enhanced Gaussian colours from training views corrected by a per-view colour transform and tone curve, and LITA-GS~ Zhou2025LITAGS renders an illumination map from per-Gaussian features, guided by illumination-invariant structure priors. These models have two limitations. First, a curve applied uniformly over a view, as in Luminance-GS, maps each observed intensity to the same output wherever it occurs. Unless the darkening is global, a dark object beside a lamp and a bright object in an unlit corner may record the same value, yet need different corrections (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Second, a spatially varying degradation stored in the Gaussians, as in Gaussian-DK and LITA-GS, has the same resolution as the scene, so it can become entangled with scene detail. These limitations raise a key question: can low-light degradation be modelled as a spatially varying, physically motivated quantity that is inferred from each view rather than learned for it, yet coarse enough to leave the scene's texture to the Gaussians? To answer it, we propose VeilGS, which treats low-light degradation as a veil drawn over a well-lit scene (Fig.~ fig:teaser ): the Gaussians hold the clean scene, and the veil holds the darkness. First, we replace the spherical harmonics of each Gaussian with an albedo and a shading latent, so that the effect of light is separable from the physical colour of the object, following Retinex theory~ Land1977Retinex . Second, we model the veil as a spatially varying gain followed by a global camera tone curve, and span the gain with a coarse basis that a small network reads off the observation. Third, rather than learning per-view coefficients for this basis, we solve for them from each observation with a differentiable bilinear rank-one solver. Finally, we train the scene through the solve, which discourages the Gaussians from absorbing what the veil can explain, in the spirit of variable projection~ Golub1973VarPro . VeilGS needs no paired normal-light supervision, stores no per-image parameters, and renders the restored scene without the veil. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose VeilGS, an unsupervised 3DGS framework for low-light novel view synthesis that models the degradation as a veil drawn over a well-lit scene. We replace per-Gaussian spherical harmonics with an albedo and a shading latent, with priors on each that encourage separating surface colour from the effect of light, producing a restored radiance for the veil to act on. We represent the veil as a coarse, spatially varying gain kept outside the Gaussians and solved from each observation, and train the scene through this solve, in the spirit of variable projection. To our knowledge, VeilGS is the first low-light 3DGS method that solves, rather than stores, its per-view degradation. Extensive experiments on the LOM and Gaussian-DK benchmarks and a user study with 55 participants demonstrate that VeilGS compares favourably with state-of-the-art NeRF- and 3DGS-based low-light methods. NeRF~ Mildenhall2021NeRF renders an implicit field by volume rendering and assumes well-exposed, photometrically consistent inputs. When the lighting changes across views, NeRF-W~ MartinBrualla2021NeRFW absorbs the change into per-view appearance embeddings, and BilaRF~ Wang2024BilaRF into per-view bilateral grids that mimic the camera pipeline. Both reproduce the lighting of the inputs rather than restore it. RAW-NeRF~ Mildenhall2022RawNeRF recovers dark scenes, but only from RAW data. For dark sRGB captures, later methods model the darkness itself. LLNeRF~ Wang2023LLNeRF decomposes each point into view-independent and view-dependent components, and Aleth-NeRF~ Cui2024AlethNeRF explains darkness with concealing fields that are removed at test time. RoSe~ Li2025RoSe estimates an illumination transition in 3D, and I -NeRF~ Liu2025I2NeRF models light--media interactions with a unified radiative equation. VeilGS takes a third route: its veil varies across the image but stays coarse and outside the Gaussians, and is solved from each view's image rather than learned. Learned Bases and Differentiable Solvers A common way to keep a per-image quantity simple is to write it in a small basis. Camera responses are well described by a low-dimensional linear basis~ Grossberg2003EMoR , and HDRNet~ Gharbi2017HDRNet infers a coarse grid of local affine coefficients from a downsampled input. BA-Net~ Tang2019BANet and Tang~ ~ Tang2022ZIC go further and solve for the coefficients rather than predict them. Solving for the linear coefficients in closed form and optimizing only the remaining parameters is classical variable projection~ Golub1973VarPro,Ruhe1980Separable . Gradients can pass through such a solve by argmin differentiation~ Gould2016Argmin , optimization layers~ Amos2017OptNet or closed-form ridge regression~ Bertinetto2019R2D2 , so the networks around it can be trained end to end. These solvers are, however, typically trained with ground-truth supervision. VeilGS places such a solve inside the optimization of a 3D scene, where neither the scene nor its degradation has ground truth.
